title: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in medical imaging: a systematic review of techniques, applications, and challenges
key_finding: PRISMA 2020 systematic review of XAI across radiology (X-ray, CT, MRI), digital pathology and multimodal imaging; searched PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Springer, Elsevier, Wiley and ACM for 2015-2025; 980 records reduced to 133 included studies (Cohen kappa 0.82 and 0.79 for screening stages). Modality scope: all imaging. Explanation families: attribution/saliency (Grad-CAM, LRP, integrated gradients, occlusion), attention, model-agnostic (LIME, SHAP), rule-based/symbolic; counterfactuals only mentioned briefly; concept-based, prototype/case-based and vision-language explanations are not treated as separate families in the text I read. Evaluation of explanations: no metric-level treatment seen; lack of standardised interpretability measures named as a gap. Own contribution: a four-family XAI taxonomy mapped to clinical workflow impact points (a reporting framework is also announced in the outline).
use_for: Prior-reviews table: general systematic review of XAI in medical imaging (all modalities, not chest CT specific)
verified_how: Crossref record + Springer full-text page (first ~100k characters; later sections not read)
flags: PMC12809972 page could not be opened (reCAPTCHA); verified through Springer and Crossref instead. Springer text read was truncated in the Applications section, so Challenges/Discussion were not checked. Page lists conference abstracts as both eligible and excluded (internal inconsistency in the source).

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Image Analysis: A Comprehensive Survey
key_finding: Narrative (non-PRISMA) survey of XAI for biomedical images; literature drawn from Scopus, PubMed, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore and Web of Science with Boolean queries, but search period and number of included papers are not stated. Modality scope: all imaging (radiography, CT, MRI, ultrasound, PET, optical, microscopy, multi-modality). Explanation families: visualisation-based (CAM, gradient/backpropagation, attention, perturbation), non-visualisation-based (example-based, concept-based, text-based) and latent-based, plus a dedicated part on multimodal and vision-language models. Evaluation: has a section summarising interpretability metrics and open-source toolkits and calls evaluation inconsistent and fragmented. Own contribution: a three-category method taxonomy and a modality-centred taxonomy mapping XAI methods to imaging types; includes its own table comparing itself with seven earlier surveys.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: broadest recent survey covering all explanation families incl. vision-language; shows that modality-wide surveys exist but none is chest-CT-specific
verified_how: arXiv abstract page + PDF pages (1, 3, 4, 26) via alphaXiv
flags: Preprint only (v1, 9 Jul 2025; PDF header says 'Manuscript submitted to ACM'); no published version found in a Crossref search. No DOI.

title: Explainable artificial intelligence for medical imaging systems using deep learning: a comprehensive review
key_finding: Comprehensive review of XAI for deep-learning medical imaging organised around frameworks, techniques and evaluation; describes a structured search (PRISMA not named) covering 2019-2024, with a final set of about 300 papers. Modality scope: all imaging (MRI, CT, chest X-ray, mammography, fundus, dermoscopy, histopathology, endoscopy). Explanation families: attribution (backpropagation, CAM/Grad-CAM, LRP, Deep SHAP, LIME, perturbation), attention, counterfactual, textual/image-captioning, concept-based (TCAV) and example/prototype-based. Evaluation: a dedicated section on evaluation methods is listed. Own contribution: comparative tables; it reuses existing taxonomies (post-hoc vs ante-hoc, local vs global, explanation type) rather than proposing a named new one.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: general XAI-in-medical-imaging review with wide method coverage but no chest-CT focus
verified_how: Crossref record + Springer full-text page (first ~100k characters)
flags: Article number not shown in Crossref record or in the page text read (null). Source is internally inconsistent: methods name PubMed/IEEE Xplore/ScienceDirect/Google Scholar in one place and Scopus/Web of Science (520 + 350 records) in another, and the introduction says 'over 200' studies while the screening text gives 300. Evaluation section itself was beyond the portion read. Crossref container-title field was empty; journal name taken from short title 'Cluster Comput' and the task brief.

title: Responsible artificial intelligence in medical imaging: a systematic review
key_finding: PRISMA-informed review of responsible AI (explainability, fairness, privacy, uncertainty, clinician trust) in imaging-based disease detection; seven databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Google Scholar), 2020-2025, 24 included studies appraised with QUADAS-2/PROBAST-AI-derived domains. Modality scope: all imaging (X-ray, CT, MRI, mammography, ultrasound, dermoscopy, fundus, OCT). Explanation families: attribution only (Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, LIME, SHAP, saliency, LRP), which dominate the evidence; concept-based, prototype, counterfactual and vision-language explanations not discussed. Evaluation of explanations: discussed as a gap (only one included study did a human-centred evaluation; most heatmaps were never checked by radiologists). Own contribution: a conceptual responsible-AI framework figure, not a formal XAI taxonomy.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: responsible-AI review where explainability is one pillar; evidence that attribution maps dominate and are rarely validated by experts
verified_how: Crossref record + Frontiers full-text page
flags: PubMed page for PMID 42535035 could not be opened; the PMID-to-article match rests on a search-result listing with the same title. Title and abstract say 'systematic review' but the full text describes itself as a 'PRISMA-informed scoping mini review'; flow diagram starts from only 55 records. Small evidence base (24 studies).

title: Current status and future directions of explainable artificial intelligence in medical imaging
key_finding: Narrative review for a radiology readership that starts from how radiologists reason (fast Type 1 versus deliberate Type 2 thinking), then surveys inherently interpretable and post-hoc XAI methods, milestones in medical imaging and commercial AI products that ship explanations such as heatmaps; concludes current XAI is not mature enough for clinical use because its outputs are hard for medical experts to interpret. Modality scope: all medical imaging / radiology. PRISMA, databases, search period and number of included studies: not stated in the abstract. Explanation families: inherent interpretability and post-hoc explanation named; finer families not stated in the abstract. Evaluation of explanations: not stated. Own framework/taxonomy: not stated; recommendation is to model clinician reasoning when designing XAI.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: radiology-journal narrative review of XAI; clinician-reasoning perspective
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + abstract read on the University of Malaya repository record for the same DOI
flags: ScienceDirect not accessible, so only the abstract (via institutional repository) was read. The brief listed this as 'European Journal of Radiology 2024': the DOI carries 2024 but Crossref gives the issue date as February 2025 (vol 183, article 111884), so year is recorded as 2025; first-online date not shown in Crossref (probably late 2024). The repository lists an 'online date' of 11 Dec 2025, which looks like a deposit date or typo.

title: A Scoping Review of Interpretable AI Model Approaches in Echocardiography: Frameworks, Model Types, Explanation Strategies, and Evaluation Practices
journal: Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine
key_finding: PRISMA-ScR/JBI scoping review of interpretable AI in echocardiography; Web of Science, PubMed, IEEE Xplore and ACM Digital Library searched on 20 May 2026 for records through 2025; 2,126 records, 170 studies included (protocol not registered). Modality scope: echocardiography only. Studies are split into multistep frameworks (interpretable intermediate representation, usually CNN upstream plus transparent downstream model) and end-to-end frameworks (mostly CNN with CAM-type maps). Explanation families: attribution (CAM/Grad-CAM/Grad-CAM++, attention, occlusion, SHAP, LIME), intrinsically interpretable models, rare case-based methods; concept-bottleneck, counterfactual and vision-language explanations are not listed as categories. Evaluation: central theme - explanations coded as functionally, human-, application- or only qualitatively grounded; qualitative-only evaluation in 23/57 (40.4%) end-to-end instances versus 2/122 (1.6%) multistep. Own contribution: multistep versus end-to-end framing and an operational coding table for evaluation categories.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: same target journal; modality-specific scoping review with explicit audit of how explanations are evaluated - a template for what is missing for chest CT
verified_how: Crossref record + Springer article page (abstract and methods)
flags: Online-first: no volume/issue/pages assigned in Crossref (Springer metadata shows pages 1-66, not recorded as final). Author list taken from Crossref (4 authors); the Springer page truncated the list.

title: Detecting and Mitigating the Clever Hans Effect in Medical Imaging: A Scoping Review
journal: Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine
key_finding: Scoping review of shortcut learning (Clever Hans effect) in medical imaging: 173 papers from 2010-2024 examined, 37 analysed in detail. Detection approaches are grouped as model-centric, data-centric, and uncertainty/bias-based; mitigation approaches as data manipulation, feature disentanglement/suppression, and domain-knowledge-driven. Main message: most medical imaging ML studies neither test for nor report shortcut learning, and the authors call for standardised benchmarks and automated detection tools. Modality scope: all medical imaging. PRISMA/PRISMA-ScR use and databases searched: not stated in the abstract. Explanation families covered: not stated in the abstract (attribution methods such as Grad-CAM and SHAP appear in the reference list). Evaluation of explanations: not the focus; it reviews validation of models against spurious cues. Own contribution: a two-level categorisation of detection and mitigation methods.
use_for: Prior-reviews table and the section on explanations as a tool for finding shortcuts/spurious features; same target journal
verified_how: Crossref record + Springer article page (abstract, metadata and reference list only)
flags: Full text is paywalled: methods and results were NOT read, so database names, PRISMA status and the role of saliency methods in detection are unverified. First online 25 Nov 2024; assigned to vol 38 issue 4 (August 2025) - year recorded as 2025 by issue.

title: A critical review of explainable deep learning in lung cancer diagnosis
key_finding: PRISMA-guided critical review of explainable deep learning for lung cancer across CT, chest radiography, histopathology whole-slide images, EBUS and PET/CT; Scopus, IEEE and PubMed searched for January 2020 to November 2024; 434 records, 147 assessed for eligibility, of which 102 only mentioned explainability without applying it. Most included work is classification (n=31) and histopathology is the commonest modality (n=19), not CT. Explanation families: attribution/saliency and the CAM family, attention, SHAP/LIME feature methods; concept-based, prototype, counterfactual and vision-language explanations are not reviewed as families. Evaluation: discussed - clinician involvement is rare, inter-observer variability complicates scoring of maps, and only six articles compared XAI methods with each other. Own contribution: four focus areas (clinician involvement, clinical interpretation, translation, adaptation of methods to lung imaging) and comparison tables, no formal new taxonomy seen.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: closest disease-specific prior review (lung cancer); shows gap - multi-modality, attribution-centred, pre-2025 search, no concept/prototype/VLM coverage
verified_how: Crossref record + Springer full-text page (first ~100k characters)
flags: Final number of included studies is not stated explicitly in the text read (counts in the text imply roughly 44-45). Discussion section was cut off. A second attempt to read the methods section was rate-limited (HTTP 429). Online 9 Dec 2025, issue dated January 2026.

title: Explainable AI in Cancer Imaging: Scoping Review of Methods, Modalities, and Clinical Integration
key_finding: PRISMA-ScR scoping review (search reported with PRISMA-S) of XAI in radiological cancer imaging; PubMed and Scopus, 2017 to December 2024; 371 studies included from 2,324 screened. Modality scope: radiology only (CT 37.5%, MRI 28%, plus ultrasound, mammography, X-ray, PET-CT; histopathology and dermoscopy excluded); lung is the second commonest site (23.5%) after breast (30.2%). Explanation families (Arrieta taxonomy): visualisation-based maps (163 studies) and feature relevance such as SHAP/LIME (111) dominate; explanation by example incl. prototypes and counterfactuals (6), text explanations (7), concept/prototype/causal designs (7), intrinsically interpretable models (21); post hoc methods are 82.2% of the field. Evaluation: 178/371 (48%) reported no validation of the explanation at all; among the 193 that did, 53.9% used expert/user judgement and only 5.2% quantitative metrics. Own contribution: four inductively derived validation categories; no new XAI taxonomy. Code shared in 17.5% and decision-support integration reported in 12.1% of studies.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: largest recent radiology-restricted XAI review with CT as leading modality; quantitative evidence that explanations are rarely validated
verified_how: JMIR publisher full-text page (first ~100k characters)
flags: Crossref record not opened (metadata from publisher page only); NLM abbreviation not seen. Final part of Discussion (limitations) not read.

title: Self-eXplainable AI for medical image analysis: A survey and new outlooks
key_finding: Survey of self-explainable (inherently interpretable) deep models for medical image analysis, covering more than 200 papers from 2018 to October 2024 taken from major ML/vision/MICCAI venues and top journals (no PRISMA, no database search). Modality scope: all imaging (X-ray, CT/MRI, dermatology, pathology, retinal, ultrasound). Explanation families: knowledge-graph and feature-engineering inputs; attention-based, concept-based (supervised, automatically discovered, generative) and prototype-based (explicit/implicit) models; textual explanations incl. medical vision-language models; self-explaining counterfactual generation. Post-hoc attribution is deliberately out of scope and criticised for doubtful fidelity. Evaluation: dedicated section on desired characteristics of explanations and on application-, human- and functionally grounded evaluation. Own contribution: an input / model / output explainability taxonomy plus tables of reviewed methods and more than 70 public datasets (notes LIDC-IDRI nodule attributes as a concept-learning resource for CT).
use_for: Prior-reviews table: the reference review for concept-based, prototype-based and other interpretable-by-design models; contrast with attribution-centred reviews
verified_how: Crossref record for the journal version (title, authors, volume, article number) + arXiv abstract page + arXiv v2 PDF pages via alphaXiv
flags: Content details were read from the arXiv version v2 (Nov 2024), not from the Information Fusion version of record (ScienceDirect not accessible; arXiv v3 dated 26 Sep 2026 exists) - the published text may differ. Crossref gives issue date March 2027 (vol 139) with the record created 15 Sep 2026; exact first-online day not shown, so online_date is given as month only. First preprint appeared in Oct 2024.

title: Which explainable AI methods in medical imaging are clinically impactful? A systematic literature review addressing the clinician's perspective
key_finding: PRISMA 2020 systematic review, registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261301196), of studies in which healthcare professionals evaluated XAI for medical imaging; Medline, Web of Science, IEEE, ACM Digital Library and Scopus searched from inception to 17 November 2025 with an information specialist; 9,305 records, 51 studies included; designs classified with MMAT and risk of bias assessed. Modality scope: all medical imaging. Explanation families compared: attribution-based, example-based and concept-based. Finding: clinician-centred evaluation is growing but methodologically fragile; example- and concept-based explanations were associated with gains on subjective and objective measures and on automation-bias assessments, whereas attribution maps mainly improved clinician perception with unclear effect on decisions. Evaluation of explanations is the subject of the review. Own framework/taxonomy: not stated in the abstract.
use_for: Prior-reviews table and evaluation section: best current evidence on human-centred evaluation of explanation types
verified_how: Crossref record including abstract
flags: Only the Crossref-deposited abstract was read, not the full text. PubMed page (PMID 42290694) could not be opened. Prototype, counterfactual and vision-language coverage not stated in the abstract.

title: Explainable artificial intelligence in medical imaging: how to interpret, evaluate, and use artificial intelligence explanations
key_finding: Educational narrative review written for practising radiologists on how to question, appraise and act on AI explanations across detection, segmentation and classification. Modality scope: radiology / all imaging. Not systematic: no PRISMA, databases, period or study count. Explanation families: saliency (Grad-CAM variants, LRP, integrated gradients), LIME/SHAP, concept-based (TCAV, ACE), example-based (counterfactuals, prototype models), ante-hoc versus post-hoc designs, a short look at natural-language explanations from vision-language models, and uncertainty quantification as a complement. Evaluation: a major theme - separates plausibility from faithfulness, covers sanity checks, pointing game and insertion/deletion scores, and notes the absence of standard metrics. Own contribution: clinician-facing critical questions, a three-phase workflow and a goal-driven guide to choosing a method; no formal checklist. Stresses that explanations are oversight tools, not proof of correctness.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: most recent radiology-journal review covering all explanation families and evaluation, but narrative and not chest-CT-specific
verified_how: Publisher (dirjournal.org) full-text article page
flags: Crossref lookup for this DOI was rate-limited (HTTP 429), so metadata come from the publisher page only. E-published ahead of print 21 Aug 2026: volume, issue and pages not yet assigned. Contents of the tables were not visible in the text read.

title: Beyond Post hoc Explanations: A Comprehensive Framework for Accountable AI in Medical Imaging Through Transparency, Interpretability, and Explainability
key_finding: PRISMA 2020 systematic review with meta-analysis of post hoc explanation quality; PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library and Web of Science, January 2019 to December 2024; 847 records, 67 studies pooled (23 radiology, 19 pathology, 25 ophthalmology). Modality scope: radiology, pathology and ophthalmology. Explanation families analysed: only LIME, SHAP and Grad-CAM (prototype models appear in background; concept-based, counterfactual and text explanations not analysed). Reports pooled fidelity of 0.81 for LIME, 0.54 for Grad-CAM and 0.38 for SHAP, marked instability of SHAP under 10% noise in ophthalmology (rho 0.42) versus radiology (rho 0.89), and a 5-7% AUC cost for interpretable models. Evaluation of explanations is the core subject (fidelity as correlation with occlusion sensitivity; stability as rank correlation under noise). Own contribution: a three-pillar accountability framework (transparency, interpretability, cautious post hoc explanation with uncertainty) with risk-stratified deployment guidance.
use_for: Prior-reviews table and evaluation section: an attempt at quantitative synthesis of fidelity/stability of post hoc methods; supports the argument against relying on heatmaps alone
verified_how: Crossref record + MDPI full-text page
flags: Treat the pooled numbers with caution: the page does not clearly explain how stability values were pooled across studies, section 4.2 gives LIME/SHAP fidelity as '30-40%' which conflicts with the abstract values, and the conclusions mention clinical validation although no clinical outcome data are reported. Cite as the authors' reported estimates, not as established effect sizes.

title: Vision-language foundation models for medical imaging: a review of current practices and innovations
key_finding: Narrative-synthesis review (no PRISMA) of medical vision-language foundation models, based on Google Scholar and arXiv searches for 2020-2024 (preprints 2022-2024) and covering 61 models. Modality scope: all imaging (X-ray, CT, fundus, MRI, pathology, ultrasound and others), with a CT subsection that covers CT-CLIP/CT-RATE, 3D-CT-GPT, E3D-GPT and Merlin. Explainability: named as a focus and noted for individual models, but there is no systematic treatment of explanation methods (attribution, concept, prototype, counterfactual not reviewed as families; text output is the implicit explanation). Evaluation of explanations: not discussed. Own contribution: a taxonomy by modality, anatomical target, task type and data source, split into specific-domain and multi-domain models.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: vision-language foundation-model review that includes chest CT models but leaves explainability and its evaluation largely unaddressed
verified_how: Crossref record + Springer open-access article page
flags: Abstract states a 2022-2024 window while the inclusion criteria state 2020-2024 for peer-reviewed work.

title: Vision Foundation Models in Radiology: A Scoping Review of Data, Methodology, Evaluation and Clinical Translation
key_finding: PRISMA-ScR scoping review (protocol not registered) of imaging-only foundation models in radiology; PubMed, Scopus, IEEE and EMBASE searched in March 2026 for peer-reviewed papers from January 2017 to March 2026; 2,596 records, 67 studies included; vision-language models were excluded by design. Modality scope: radiology (brain MRI, thoracoabdominal CT and chest X-ray dominate; 12 CT-only studies). Studies were scored against the FUTURE-AI principles: explainability was addressed in 48/67 (71.6%), less often than robustness (94%), and where present was mostly limited to post hoc activation or saliency maps; fairness in 50.7%. Explanation families beyond post hoc maps: not covered. Evaluation of explanations: not examined beyond noting the reliance on post hoc visualisation. Own contribution: a three-pillar evidence-mapping framework (data scale/heterogeneity, pretraining/architecture, downstream transferability).
use_for: Prior-reviews table and foundation-model section: evidence that radiology foundation models treat explainability as an afterthought (post hoc maps only)
verified_how: arXiv v1 PDF full text read via alphaXiv (title, authors, abstract, methods, results, discussion)
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed (8 Jul 2026); no journal version found. Authors are employees of an imaging company (declared competing interest). Not a vision-language review - language-based models were excluded.

title: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in deep learning-based medical image analysis
key_finding: Standard reference survey of XAI for deep-learning medical image analysis: introduces a framework of XAI criteria for classifying methods, then sorts the surveyed papers by that framework and by anatomical location, and closes with future opportunities. Modality scope: all imaging. PRISMA, databases, period and number of included papers: not stated in the abstract. Explanation families: not listed in the abstract (a later survey's comparison table, Dagnaw et al. 2025, rates it as covering gradient-, perturbation-, example- and text-based methods fully and CAM, attention and concept-based methods only partially, with no coverage of vision-language models). Evaluation of explanations: not stated in the abstract (rated as partially covered by Dagnaw et al.). Own contribution: the criteria-based classification framework.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: the highly cited baseline survey (pre-2025 essential original) against which newer reviews position themselves
verified_how: Crossref record (journal metadata) + arXiv abstract page of the same paper (journal reference and DOI shown there)
flags: Older than 2025 (included as the one standard survey). Only the abstract was read; ScienceDirect not accessible. Method-family coverage is quoted second-hand from the Dagnaw et al. comparison table, not checked in the full text. Online date 2022-05-04 is inferred by Crossref licence/created dates, not an explicit field.

title: Medical slice transformer for improved diagnosis and explainability on 3D medical images with DINOv2
key_finding: Task: lung nodule malignancy classification on chest CT (LIDC-IDRI, 722 patients, 1,625 nodules), alongside breast MRI and knee MRI tasks. Model: a slice-wise DINOv2 encoder with a Transformer aggregator (MST) compared with a 3D ResNet-50; explanations were transformer attention maps for MST and Grad-CAM for the ResNet. Explanation evaluation: one radiologist blindly rated 50 maps per dataset (150 in total) for whether the map marked the correct slice and the lesion core; attention maps hit the correct slice in 136/150 and the lesion core in 57/150, against 37/150 and 0/150 for Grad-CAM; no overlap metric was used, and the chest CT AUC gain (0.95 vs 0.92) was not significant.
use_for: Attention maps vs Grad-CAM on 3D CT; example of reader-rated saliency evaluation for nodule malignancy
verified_how: nature.com full text (open access) + Crossref record
flags: Saliency rating came from a single reader and pooled three datasets, of which chest CT is only one; per-dataset rating counts were not extracted.

title: A multi-view CNN model to predict resolving of new lung nodules on follow-up low-dose chest CT
key_finding: Task: predicting whether new intermediate-sized solid nodules found at lung cancer screening will resolve at follow-up low-dose CT. Cohort: 344 nodules in 250 participants of the NELSON trial (63 resolving), four-fold cross-validation and no external test set. Model: a multi-view CNN combining three 2D ResNet-18 branches and one 3D ResNet-18 (AUC 0.81); Grad-CAM++ heat maps were shown for four example cases only, so the explanation was shown qualitatively only.
use_for: Lung nodule management in screening; typical display-only use of Grad-CAM++
verified_how: Springer landing page (open access full text) + Crossref record
flags: No external validation (acknowledged by the authors).

title: Explainable deep learning-based lung cancer diagnosis using clinically-guided local interpretable model-agnostic explanations
key_finding: Task: classifying lung CT slices as normal, benign or malignant on the public IQ-OTH/NCCD set (1,097 slices from 110 patients) with a custom 11-layer CNN. Explanation: ASP-LIME, a LIME variant with adaptive superpixels, stratified perturbation sampling and lung-region masking, compared with LIME, Grad-CAM, SmoothGrad and others. Explanation evaluation: quantitative faithfulness and stability tests, with deletion 0.030, insertion 0.962 and ABPC 0.966, perturbation RMSE 0.87 vs 3.25 for LIME, and repeat-run SSIM 0.78 over 90 test slices; no reader study.
use_for: LIME on chest CT; example of deletion/insertion and stability testing of explanations
verified_how: nature.com full text (open access); Crossref record could not be opened (server errors, then rate limit)
flags: Author list taken from the nature.com byline, which renders an ellipsis before the last author; in two other Scientific Reports pages opened this session the same rendering hid no names, so the seven names are probably complete, but this was not confirmed against Crossref; surname/initial parsing of 'Shahab Ul Hassan' is uncertain. Journal abbreviation taken from other Crossref records of the same journal. Train/validation split was at slice level without patient identifiers, so the 99.84% accuracy may be inflated by leakage; the deletion improvement over LIME was not significant (p = 0.32) although the Discussion says all gains were significant.

title: LungCraft: a hybrid 3D-2D deep learning and radiomics framework with explainable AI for precision diagnosis of lung cancer
key_finding: Task: benign versus malignant classification of lung lesions on CT with a two-stream network (3D CNN on patches plus 2D EfficientNet-B0 on slices) fused with 14 radiomic features; trained on 61 TCIA volumes and tested externally on LIDC-IDRI and NSCLC-Radiomics (reported AUC 0.91 and 0.92). Explanation: Grad-CAM for spatial localisation and KernelSHAP for the radiomic features. Explanation evaluation: two raters judged the clinical relevance of Grad-CAM maps in 6 cases (Cohen kappa 0.45, 83.3% raw agreement) and two blinded reviewers scored a five-point 'interpretability index' (ICC 0.79); no faithfulness metric was reported.
use_for: Grad-CAM plus SHAP in a hybrid model; small-scale rater assessment of heat maps
verified_how: Frontiers full text (open access) + Crossref record
flags: Very small development set (about 43/9/9 patients) and an acknowledged overfitting risk; the rater assessment covered only 6 cases; the page text describes LIDC-IDRI inconsistently (1,018 patients vs 1,018 images). The last ~10% of the page text was not read.

title: Interpretable Deep Learning with Multi-Scale CT for Predicting Occult Lymph Node Metastasis in Early-Stage NSCLC: A Multicenter Study
journal: Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine
key_finding: Task: preoperative prediction of occult lymph node metastasis in early-stage NSCLC from CT. Cohort: 900 patients from two hospitals (500 for development, 400 as an external test cohort). Model: 3D EfficientNet with AUC 0.891 internally and 0.872 externally, higher than comparison CNNs and four radiologists. Explanation: Grad-CAM, reported in the abstract only as showing distinct attention patterns; evaluation of explanation not stated.
use_for: Lung cancer staging; multicentre study where Grad-CAM is reported without stated validation
verified_how: Springer landing page (abstract) + Crossref record
flags: Full text is paywalled, so only the abstract was read and the methods could not be checked for any assessment of the Grad-CAM maps. Online-first article with no volume or issue; Springer metadata shows provisional pages 1-13. Abbreviation is the Crossref short-container-title as shown.

title: Multi-center validated attention-BiFPN deep learning for CT-based lung cancer subtype classification
key_finding: Task: distinguishing lung adenocarcinoma from squamous cell carcinoma on CT slices. Cohort: 290 patients from two centres (200 for training with cross-validation, 90 held out as an external test set with only 28 squamous cases). Model: ResNet18 with self- and cross-attention and a BiFPN, fed with slices on which radiologist-drawn lesion masks are overlaid (external AUC 0.989). Explanation: Grad-CAM, judged by visual inspection of correct and misclassified cases against the annotated tumour area; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: Lung cancer histological subtype; multicentre study with qualitative Grad-CAM
verified_how: Springer landing page (open access full text); Crossref record could not be opened (rate limit)
flags: Crossref not opened, so journal abbreviation and issue are null. Near-perfect internal cross-validation results (AUC 1.000) and reliance on manual lesion masks as input; small squamous sample in the external set.

title: An explainable multimodal 2.5D deep learning-radiomics model for predicting extranodal extension in lung adenocarcinoma using preoperative CT: a multicenter retrospective cohort study
key_finding: Task: predicting pathological extranodal extension in lung adenocarcinoma from preoperative chest CT. Cohort: 274 patients for training at one centre and 95 for external validation at two others. Model: logistic regression on 19 selected features combining intratumoral and peritumoral radiomics with ResNet-18 deep features from five axial slices (AUC 0.88 training, 0.78 external). Explanation: SHAP ranking, summary and dependence plots for the features, with Grad-CAM heat maps given as figure examples; explanation shown qualitatively only, with no fidelity, stability or reader assessment.
use_for: Lung cancer staging; SHAP on a deep-radiomics model with Grad-CAM as illustration
verified_how: Springer landing page (open access full text) + Crossref record
flags: The middle authors were hidden on the Springer page; the full list is from Crossref. SHAP explains the fused feature model, not the image voxels.

title: CT-based deep learning model for improved disease-free survival prediction in clinical stage I lung cancer: a real-world multicenter study
key_finding: Task: predicting disease-free survival in clinical stage I NSCLC from pre-treatment CT. Cohort: 2,489 surgically treated patients for development and internal testing, plus 248 patients treated with stereotactic body radiotherapy at two hospitals for external validation. Model: 3D CNN risk score with C-index 0.85 on the internal test set versus 0.76 for a clinical Cox model, and significant risk stratification in the radiotherapy cohort. Explanation: Grad-CAM is listed among the abbreviations and cited, but the abstract does not describe it; evaluation of explanation not stated.
use_for: Lung cancer prognosis; large multicentre study in which the saliency analysis is not reported in the abstract
verified_how: Springer landing page (abstract, abbreviations and reference list) + Crossref record
flags: Full text is paywalled: Grad-CAM use is inferred from the abbreviation list and the reference to Selvaraju et al., and how it was applied or assessed could not be read. Confirm in the full text before citing it as a Grad-CAM study.

title: An efficient dual path deep learning framework for COVID-19 classification using lung CT scans with explainable AI
key_finding: Task: COVID-19 versus normal classification of lung CT images pooled from nine public sources (25,408 images: 16,341 COVID-19 and 9,067 normal; split at patient level). Model: a lightweight parallel network joining a pretrained MobileNetV2 branch and a custom CNN (accuracy 97.46%, AUC 0.994), benchmarked against CNNs and vision transformers. Explanation: Grad-CAM and LIME, checked on two CT images with radiologist-marked ground-glass opacities taken from a published review; explanation shown qualitatively only, and a blinded radiologist comparison is named as future work.
use_for: COVID-19 CT; paired Grad-CAM and LIME without quantitative validation
verified_how: nature.com full text (open access) + Crossref record
flags: No cross-dataset validation; small inconsistencies between reported accuracy figures in the text (97.41%, 97.46%, 97.51%).

title: Multimodal text guided network for chest CT pneumonia classification
key_finding: Task: three-class classification of chest CT sequences into viral pneumonia, bacterial pneumonia and healthy, using a single-centre dataset of CT sequences paired with report text (32 slices per patient; total size not stated in the text read). Model: MTGNet, a graph-pooling CT encoder with a text-guided branch used only in training (accuracy 0.944 vs 0.919 for the CT-only baseline). Explanation: Grad-CAM heat maps for two cases; explanation shown qualitatively only, with no localisation metric or expert review.
use_for: Pneumonia aetiology on CT; display-only Grad-CAM
verified_how: nature.com full text (open access), including the Authors and Affiliations section
flags: Crossref record not opened; journal abbreviation taken from the article page. Dataset size is given only in a table that was not visible. Single-centre data without external validation.

title: Deep learning for classifying imaging patterns of interstitial lung disease associated with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies
key_finding: Task: five-class classification of HRCT patterns (NSIP, OP, NSIP+OP, UIP, DAD) in interstitial lung disease associated with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies. Cohort: 629 patients from one hospital (361 training, 156 internal test, 112 temporal validation). Model: 3D ResNet with a class activation mapping (CAM) attention module (AUC 0.885 internal, 0.835 temporal validation). Explanation: CAM heat maps for five randomly chosen validation patients, said to match radiologists' regions of interest; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: Interstitial lung disease pattern classification; CAM used both as an attention module and as the displayed explanation
verified_how: nature.com full text (open access) + Crossref record
flags: The method is CAM built into the network and trained with an attention loss, not Grad-CAM applied after training, so it is only partly a post hoc explanation. The 'external' set is a later time period at the same hospital.

title: Predicting Risk of Pulmonary Fibrosis Formation in PASC Patients
journal: 2025 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Computer, Data Sciences and Applications (ACDSA)
key_finding: Task: predicting CT findings suggestive of pulmonary fibrosis in patients with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19. Cohort: 347 chest CT scans from two sites (233 from the University of Pennsylvania, 114 from Istanbul hospitals; 156 positive), labelled by one thoracic radiologist. Model: 2D CNNs trained from scratch on selected axial slices with patient-level majority voting (DenseNet-121 accuracy 82.2%, ResNet-18 AUC 85.5%), plus radiomics models (best AUC 72.5%). Explanation: Grad-CAM on DenseNet-121, described as concordant with fibrotic regions; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: Post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis; two-site data with display-only Grad-CAM
verified_how: arXiv abstract page + full text via alphaXiv + Crossref record of the IEEE proceedings version + university publication record
flags: Conference paper (IEEE, 6 pages); the full text read was the arXiv version, which may differ from the IEEE version. online_date is the arXiv submission date; the proceedings date in Crossref is 2025-08-07. Both sites were pooled for cross-validation, so there is no held-out external centre.

title: Early identification of PRISm from chest CT: a multimodal for three-class stratification of normal, PRISm, and COPD
key_finding: Task: three-class classification of normal spirometry, preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm) and COPD from thin-slice chest CT. Cohort: 776 participants at one hospital (465/154/157 split) and 190 at a second hospital as an external test set. Model: attention-based multi-instance learning with a ResNet34 backbone plus a demographic branch (AUC 0.879 internal, 0.808 external). Explanation: Grad-CAM on representative slices, inspected visually for focus on lung parenchyma rather than chest wall or table; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: COPD and pre-COPD on CT; external validation with qualitative Grad-CAM
verified_how: Frontiers full text (open access) + Crossref record
flags: Frontiers page gives an earlier online date (2026-06-05) than Crossref (2026-07-01). The multimodal gain over CT alone is small (AUC 0.879 vs 0.873) and performance dropped externally, mostly for PRISm.

title: Deep learning based CT images for lung function prediction in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
key_finding: Task: regression of five spirometry measures (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC and percent-predicted values) from chest CT in COPD. Cohort: single-centre retrospective data, 2,408 participants in the Results (the abstract states 3,108), with 10-fold cross-validation. Model: DenseNet image encoder fused with demographic and radiomic features (Pearson r 0.84 for FEV1 and 0.81 for FVC). Explanation: Grad-CAM overlays for two example patients, described as centred on peribronchial and lower-lung tissue; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: COPD lung function from CT; display-only Grad-CAM in a regression model
verified_how: Springer landing page (open access full text) + Crossref record
flags: Cohort size differs between abstract (3,108) and Results (2,408); no external validation.

title: A deep learning model for the interpretable identification of pulmonary thromboembolism from computed tomography pulmonary angiography
key_finding: Task: detecting acute pulmonary thromboembolism on CT pulmonary angiography. Cohort: 1,368 age- and sex-matched patients (684 with emboli) split 70/30 for training and internal testing, plus 98 patients from three other hospitals as an external test set. Model: YOLOv11 detector with slice scores averaged per patient (AUC 0.777 internal and 0.778 external; detection mAP@0.5 of 0.67). Explanation: Grad-CAM overlays said to confirm attention to intravascular filling defects; explanation shown qualitatively only, with no comparison against the annotated emboli.
use_for: Pulmonary embolism; multicentre CTPA study with qualitative Grad-CAM
verified_how: Frontiers full text (open access) + Crossref record
flags: Modest diagnostic performance, and different operating thresholds were used for the internal and external cohorts.

title: AI-assisted differentiation of nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease from colonization: a multi-center study
key_finding: Task: separating nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease from colonisation in patients with respiratory NTM isolates. Cohort: 413 patients at one hospital (291/67/55 split) and 196 external patients at a second hospital. Model: NTMNet, a 3D CNN on chest CT fused with an MLP on clinical variables (AUC 0.85 internal, 0.82 external). Explanation: Grad-CAM combined with integrated gradients for the CT branch and SHAP for the clinical variables; heat maps were shown for two representative cases, so the explanation was shown qualitatively only.
use_for: Mycobacterial lung disease; combined Grad-CAM, integrated gradients and SHAP in a multimodal model
verified_how: Springer landing page (open access full text) + Crossref record
flags: Concerns NTM disease, not tuberculosis itself. Reader comparison used only 20 external patients.

title: Deep learning-based differentiation of non-tuberculous mycobacterial lung disease and pulmonary tuberculosis using chest CT
key_finding: Task: distinguishing non-tuberculous mycobacterial lung disease from pulmonary tuberculosis on chest CT. Cohort: 409 microbiologically confirmed patients from one hospital, split 329 for training and 80 for testing, with no external validation. Model: 3D ResNeXt after nnU-Net lung segmentation (test AUC 0.83), compared with six other 3D architectures. Explanation: Grad-CAM in three planes for representative cases, said to highlight bronchiectasis and tree-in-bud opacities for NTM and thick-walled cavities for tuberculosis; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: Tuberculosis versus NTM on CT; single-centre study with qualitative Grad-CAM
verified_how: Frontiers full text (open access) + Crossref record
flags: Single centre, no external test; the ablation table (AUC 0.79) does not match the main test result (AUC 0.83).

title: Imitating Radiological Scrolling: A Global-Local Attention Model for 3D Chest CT Volumes Multi-Label Anomaly Classification
journal: Proceedings of The 8th International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning (MIDL 2025), Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
key_finding: Task: multi-label classification of 18 abnormalities on 3D non-contrast chest CT. Data: CT-RATE (17,799 training, 1,314 validation and 1,314 test patients) with cross-dataset testing on 1,344 Rad-ChestCT scans. Model: CT-Scroll, a ResNet over slice triplets followed by alternating global and sliding-window attention (AUROC 81.8 on CT-RATE, 71.2 on Rad-ChestCT). Explanation: Grad-CAM maps from the ResNet backbone shown for example abnormalities in one figure; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: Multi-abnormality classification on 3D chest CT; Grad-CAM limited to the 2D slice encoder

Year follows the PMLR citation (volume 301 published 2026-05-18); the conference was held in July 2025 and the arXiv version dates from March 2025, which is recorded as online_date. No DOI.

title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
key_finding: Introduces Grad-CAM, which weights the feature maps of the last convolutional layer by the gradients of a target class score to give a coarse heat map of the image regions behind a prediction. The method needs no architectural change, applies to classification, captioning and visual question answering networks, and is reported to help users judge model reliability.
use_for: Essential original: definition of Grad-CAM
verified_how: Springer landing page + Crossref record
flags: Pre-2025 essential original (journal version of the ICCV 2017 paper).

title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
journal: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NIPS 2017)
key_finding: Proposes SHAP, a framework that assigns each input feature an importance value for an individual prediction. It shows that a class of additive feature-importance measures has a unique solution with desirable properties and that this class covers six earlier explanation methods.
use_for: Essential original: definition of SHAP
verified_how: NeurIPS proceedings abstract page
flags: Pre-2025 essential original. Page numbers and editors are not shown on the proceedings page; no DOI.

title: "Why Should I Trust You?": Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier
journal: Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
key_finding: Introduces LIME, which explains a single prediction of any classifier by fitting a simple interpretable model in the neighbourhood of that prediction. It adds a submodular selection step to choose a small, non-redundant set of representative explanations and demonstrates the approach on text and image classifiers.
use_for: Essential original: definition of LIME
verified_how: Crossref record + arXiv abstract page (the ACM page could not be opened)
flags: Pre-2025 essential original. Crossref stores the title and subtitle as separate fields; the combined form here follows the arXiv page.

title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
journal: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
key_finding: States two axioms that an attribution method should satisfy, sensitivity and implementation invariance, and shows that most earlier methods violate at least one. It proposes Integrated Gradients, which accumulates gradients along a path from a baseline input to the actual input, needs no network modification, and is demonstrated on image, text and chemistry models.
use_for: Essential original: definition of Integrated Gradients
verified_how: PMLR proceedings page
flags: Pre-2025 essential original; no DOI.

title: Vision-language model-based semantic-guided imaging biomarker for lung nodule malignancy prediction
key_finding: Predicts one-year lung cancer diagnosis for CT nodules by LoRA fine-tuning of CLIP so that nine 2D views of a 50 mm nodule crop align with report-like sentences that Gemini writes from radiologist-annotated semantic features (19 features for 1,261 NLST nodules from 938 scans, plus LIDC attributes for 2,625 lesions). It reached AUROC 0.901 and AUPRC 0.776 on the NLST test set (188 cases) and AUROC 0.771, 0.861 and 0.778 on the external LUNGx, DLCS and UCLA cohorts; zero-shot prediction of the semantic features gave AUROC 0.807 for margin, 0.812 for consistency and 0.840 for pleural attachment but was poor for most internal features (for example reticulation 0.411). Concepts are expert labels used as text supervision rather than a strict bottleneck; concept prediction quality was measured, while leakage and clinician use were not tested.
use_for: language-guided concept supervision for lung nodule malignancy on CT
verified_how: PubMed record (title, journal, volume, article number, DOI, Epub date) + arXiv v3 full text via alphaXiv + EDRN publication page (author list)
flags: Crossref record and PMC full text could not be opened (client error / rate limit / reCAPTCHA). Author order taken from the arXiv v3 manuscript; the same seven names appear on the EDRN page for this PMID. Issue not shown. Numbers are from the arXiv v3 full text, which may differ slightly from the typeset article.

title: Proto-Caps: interpretable medical image classification using prototype learning and privileged information
key_finding: Capsule network in which each capsule is tied to one radiologist-defined nodule attribute and the malignancy output is built from attribute prototypes (real training examples), tested on LIDC-IDRI (2D and 3D) and CheXpert with expert attribute labels as supervision. On LIDC-IDRI it reports 93.1% within-1 malignancy accuracy in 2D (86.4% for X-Caps) and 94.3% malignancy with 95.3% mean attribute accuracy in 3D, and attribute-specific prototypes could still be learned from about 190 attribute labels. In a reader study with six radiologists, attribute scores and prototypes tended to raise diagnostic accuracy when the model was right and lower it when the model was wrong.
use_for: attribute-based lung nodule models on LIDC-IDRI; evidence on whether concept explanations help radiologists
verified_how: PeerJ article page (abstract and full-text content) + Crossref record
flags: Crossref gives no short-container-title or issue. Headline numbers were taken from the full-text content of the PeerJ page as returned by the fetch tool; confirm exact figures against the article tables before quoting.

title: A Model for the Explainable Malignancy Assessment of Pulmonary Nodules on CT Images
key_finding: Proposes an interpretable malignancy scoring model for LIDC-IDRI nodules that joins concept-based learning with a generalized additive model: the network predicts clinically meaningful nodule attributes (numerical and categorical) and a malignancy regression score, and exposes how much each attribute contributes to that score. The abstract reports competitive classification and attribute-scoring performance and attribute-diagnosis relations that agree with clinical practice, but gives no numbers; concepts are the expert LIDC attribute ratings.
use_for: concept-based (additive) malignancy scoring from LIDC-IDRI attributes
verified_how: SpringerLink article page + Crossref record; the arXiv preprint 2405.17483 (2024) with the same authors and abstract was also opened
flags: Only the abstract was read (paywalled). This is the English-language journal version of work first posted on arXiv in May 2024 (manuscript received 3 June 2024); issue is dated December 2025, online 21 February 2026. The journal is a Springer/Pleiades translation journal; check that its indexing meets the review's standard. No quantitative results available from the abstract; leakage and clinician intervention not mentioned.

title: Distilling CT Foundation Models into Editable Concept Bottlenecks for Lung Nodule Malignancy Prediction
key_finding: Builds concept bottlenecks on two frozen CT foundation models (CT-FM and FMCIB): ridge-regression heads trained on 2,610 LIDC-IDRI nodules map embeddings to eight radiologist-defined attributes, and an additive model predicts malignancy from the estimated attributes plus nodule size (trained on LUNA25, tested internally and on the external DLCS cohort). Concept fidelity was modest (cross-validated R2 0.24 vs 0.11 for subtlety and 0.17 vs 0.08 for spiculation, FMCIB vs CT-FM); concept-plus-size models reached AUROC 0.86 internally and 0.72-0.73 externally, which was no better than nodule size alone (0.73). Concept quality was quantified and controlled concept edits were demonstrated; no clinician study or leakage analysis is described in the abstract.
use_for: post hoc concept bottlenecks on 3D CT foundation models; concept fidelity and intervention for lung nodules
verified_how: arXiv abstract page
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed; no published version was found in this session. Only the abstract was read.

title: Less Annotation, More Interpretation: Prior-Guided Concept Bottleneck Models for Interpretable Cancer Imaging Diagnosis
key_finding: Hybrid concept bottleneck model that needs few instance-level concept labels: it combines a small labelled subset, class-conditional matching of concept distributions for unlabelled patients, and prior-based initialization of the concept-to-diagnosis layer, tested on CBIS-DDSM (masses and calcifications) and LIDC-IDRI pulmonary nodules with 0-100% of concept labels. With 10% of labels, mean concept AUC rose from 0.619 to 0.741 (masses), 0.650 to 0.787 (calcifications) and 0.597 to 0.642 (lung nodules) relative to a matched standard CBM, with diagnostic performance close to black-box models; zero-shot vision-language models were judged insufficient for fine-grained tumour-level concepts. Concept accuracy was the main evaluation; leakage and clinician intervention are not reported in the abstract.
use_for: reducing concept annotation cost in CBMs; LIDC-IDRI nodule concepts
verified_how: arXiv abstract page
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed; no published version found. Only the abstract was read.

title: Minimum Data, Maximum Impact: 20 annotated samples for explainable lung nodule classification
key_finding: Addresses the shortage of attribute-annotated data for attribute-based explainable nodule classifiers: a diffusion model with attribute conditioning is trained on only 20 attribute-labelled LIDC-IDRI nodules, and its synthetic images are added to the training set of an explainable classifier. Relative to training on the small real attribute-labelled set alone, attribute prediction accuracy improved by 13.4% and malignancy prediction accuracy by 1.8%. Concepts are expert LIDC attributes; no clinician evaluation or leakage analysis is described in the abstract.
use_for: scarcity of concept labels for lung nodule attribute models
verified_how: arXiv abstract page
flags: Preprint; the arXiv page showed no journal reference or comments field, and publication status could not be checked (search budget exhausted). Only the abstract was read.

title: Sparse Concept Channels in Frozen 3D CT Vision Encoders
key_finding: Probes the frozen vision embeddings of a 3D chest CT vision-language model (Pillar-0) and finds that each radiological finding is carried by roughly ten embedding channels, which match a full-feature classifier and clearly beat zero-shot text prompting. Zeroing the channels for one finding collapses that finding's score while unrelated labels stay stable, and the same sparse probe transfers to the abdominal model Merlin. A training-free probe plus a report template gave higher clinical-efficacy F1 than CT-CHAT (0.549 vs 0.184) at about 22 times lower latency; concepts here are discovered post hoc against report-derived finding labels rather than supervised in a bottleneck.
use_for: concept discovery and causal concept testing inside 3D chest CT foundation models
verified_how: alphaXiv page for the arXiv record (abstract and page body)
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed. The arxiv.org page itself was not opened; the alphaXiv mirror was. The use of CT-RATE for the chest experiments comes from the page body, not the abstract. No clinician study.

title: Auditable CT Phenotyping Through Report-derived Radiological Observations
key_finding: Introduces ACT, which predicts electronic-health-record phenotypes from CT through a bank of radiological observations mined from reports (376,194 observations; training on 38,317 patients, evaluation on 25,183 held-out patients and 221 phenotypes, including unseen CT pulmonary angiograms). ACT beat CT-CLIP (0.651 vs 0.572 zero-shot; 0.709 vs 0.662 with linear probing) and exposed shortcut reliance: only 97 observations filled the 221 top-ranked positions, and one phrase about aortic and coronary calcification ranked first for 20 phenotypes including osteoporosis and depression. Restricting the observation bank to clinician-specified evidence moved the probes onto phenotype-related observations for 86 phenotypes without loss of accuracy (0.751 vs 0.741).
use_for: report-derived concepts on 3D CT; concept layers as an audit tool for shortcuts; clinician intervention on the concept set
verified_how: alphaXiv page for the arXiv record (abstract)
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed. The alphaXiv page noted that its machine-generated overview gives a different training-corpus size (72,640 CT-report pairs) from the abstract (38,317 patients); abstract figures are used here. Author 'Barajas Ordonez F' and 'Barbosa E' are as displayed; the related medRxiv paper lists 'Eduardo Mortani Barbosa Jr'.

title: Explainability Through Human-Centric Design for XAI in Lung Cancer Detection
journal: Proceedings of the Thirty-Fourth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-25)
key_finding: Presents XpertXAI, an expert-guided concept bottleneck model (InceptionV3 backbone) for several lung pathologies on chest radiographs, trained on a public chest X-ray dataset with reports and using radiologist-defined clinical concepts. Compared against post hoc explanation methods and an unsupervised CBM (XCBs), with explanations checked against radiologist annotations for lung cancer, it gave higher predictive accuracy and concept explanations closer to expert reasoning, while the post hoc methods often missed key diagnostic features. The abstract gives no numerical results; concept alignment with experts was assessed, leakage was not discussed.
use_for: expert-defined versus unsupervised concepts in chest radiograph CBMs; clinical validity of concept explanations
verified_how: IJCAI proceedings page + arXiv abstract page
flags: Chest radiograph, not CT. Abstract reports no numbers. Publication date is that of the electronic proceedings as shown on the IJCAI page; track: Human-Centred AI.

title: Interactive Medical Image Analysis with Concept-based Similarity Reasoning
journal: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2025
key_finding: CSR learns patch-level prototypes that are each tied to a named concept (dataset finding annotations serve as concepts, disease labels as targets) and lets a doctor intervene by rejecting concepts, drawing positive or negative boxes on the image, or pruning shortcut prototypes before deployment; evaluated on two chest radiograph sets (TBX11K, VinDr-CXR) and ISIC. Macro F1 was 94.4, 54.6 and 71.5 against 88.6, 50.1 and 45.5 for a joint CBM, and the pointing-game hit rate for tuberculosis rose from 60.9% to 79.5% after a doctor refined the concept atlas. Test-time interaction by a medical student added 0.3-0.7 F1 points on TBX11K, so human intervention was tested but only at very small scale.
use_for: clinician intervention in concept models (concept-level and spatial); concept localization
verified_how: ML Anthology proceedings entry (pages, DOI, BibTeX) + arXiv abstract + arXiv v2 full text via alphaXiv
flags: Chest radiograph and dermoscopy, not CT. Pages and DOI come from the ML Anthology entry; the CVF open-access or IEEE Xplore page was not opened. Author name order follows the proceedings BibTeX (Vietnamese names; check surname convention). Interaction study involved one medical student and one non-expert.

title: MVP-CBM: Multi-layer Visual Preference-enhanced Concept Bottleneck Model for Explainable Medical Image Classification
journal: Proceedings of the Thirty-Fourth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-25)
key_finding: Language-guided CBM built on BioMedCLIP in which diagnostic-criteria concepts are generated by prompting an LLM (GPT-o1) and each concept is matched to the visual-encoder layers it aligns with best, followed by sparse fusion of concept activations across layers. On seven public datasets, including chest radiographs (MIMIC-CXR cardiomegaly, SIIM pneumothorax) and mammography (CMMD), it outperformed LaBo, post hoc CBM and Explicd, for example balanced accuracy 74.87% vs 67.12% on CMMD and 83.62% vs 81.96% on SIIM. Interpretability was shown through qualitative concept visualizations only; concept accuracy against expert labels, leakage and clinician intervention were not evaluated in the sections read.
use_for: LLM-generated concepts and vision-language CBMs in medical imaging
verified_how: IJCAI proceedings page + arXiv v1 full text via alphaXiv
flags: No chest CT data. Numbers are from the arXiv v1 full text. The paper's text says concepts may come from an LLM or human experts and the training loss includes a concept-label term; the exact source of concept labels was not clear from the pages read.

title: CoPA: Hierarchical Concept Prompting and Aggregating Network for Explainable Diagnosis
journal: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention - MICCAI 2025 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 15973)
key_finding: Argues that CBMs which read concepts only from the final encoder layer miss shallow and multi-scale cues, and proposes extracting concept-aware embeddings from every layer of the visual encoder, using them as prompts to strengthen concept-related visual features, and aligning the aggregated visual representation with textual concept embeddings. The abstract reports better concept prediction and disease prediction than prior methods on three public datasets, without naming the datasets or giving numbers.
use_for: architectural variants of language-aligned CBMs (multi-layer concept capture)
verified_how: MICCAI 2025 open-access paper page (title, authors, abstract, DOI, LNCS volume and pages)
flags: Datasets and numerical results are not given in the abstract and the full paper was not read; modality unknown from the abstract. SpringerLink page not opened.

title: Concept Complement Bottleneck Model for Interpretable Medical Image Diagnosis
journal: Proceedings of The 9th International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Targets CBMs whose expert-defined concept sets or annotations are incomplete: cross-attention modules extract features for each predefined textual concept, per-concept adapters and bottleneck layers keep concepts separated, and a complement module mines additional local concepts from a concept bank built from medical literature, so that expert-annotated and discovered concepts are learned jointly. The abstract claims better concept detection and diagnosis than existing methods but names no datasets and gives no numbers.
use_for: incomplete concept sets; combining expert-labelled and automatically discovered concepts
verified_how: PMLR proceedings page (title, authors, volume, pages, abstract)
flags: No DOI (PMLR). Datasets and results not stated in the abstract; full paper not read. Publication date within 2026 not recorded.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Information Pursuit for Interpretable and Reliable Medical Image Analysis
key_finding: Extends variational information pursuit, an interpretable-by-design method that sequentially queries an image for concepts and predicts from their answers, by accounting for per-sample uncertainty in concept predictions: one variant masks uncertain concepts and another folds uncertainty into query selection. Across five datasets in four modalities (dermoscopy, X-ray, ultrasound, blood cell imaging) the implicit variant was the most accurate interpretable-by-design approach on four datasets and used fewer concepts per explanation. The method aims to avoid unreliable concepts automatically, without human intervention.
use_for: probabilistic or uncertainty-aware concept models; reliability of concept predictions
verified_how: Crossref record (journal metadata) + alphaXiv page of the arXiv version (abstract)
flags: First author's given name is 'Md' in Crossref; initial rendered as 'M'. Abstract read from the arXiv version (v2, 22 Sep 2025), not the IEEE page; online-first date not available. Dataset names and numbers are not in the abstract. No CT data.

title: A concept-based interpretable model for the diagnosis of choroid neoplasias using multimodal data
key_finding: Multimodal concept bottleneck model for three choroidal tumour types (750 patients; fluorescein angiography, indocyanine green angiography and ultrasound) in which GPT-4 extracts candidate concepts from radiology reports, two senior ophthalmologists curate them, and each concept is grounded as a linear concept-activation vector on pretrained image features. F1 was 91.0% versus 89.2% for a black-box model (difference not significant), and precision@10 of the retrieved concepts was about 0.53-0.54. In a reader test with eight ophthalmologists, concept-based support raised the accuracy of six inexperienced doctors from 51.9% to 65.5% (F1 38.5% to 54.7%) while two senior doctors were essentially unchanged.
use_for: report-derived, LLM-extracted concepts with expert curation; evidence that concept explanations help less experienced clinicians
verified_how: Nature article page (open access full text) + Crossref record
flags: Ophthalmology, not radiology; included for the clinician evaluation and the report-to-concept pipeline. An Author Correction exists (DOI 10.1038/s41467-025-59792-1, 12 May 2025); no retraction. Reader study is small (8 readers).

title: An explainable biomedical foundation model via large-scale concept-enhanced vision–language pretraining
key_finding: ConceptCLIP is a biomedical vision-language foundation model pretrained on 23 million image-text-concept triplets (MedConcept-23M, concepts linked to UMLS) with joint image-text and region-concept alignment, and evaluated on 78 datasets across 10 imaging modalities. Besides strong diagnostic performance it yields concept-level explanations, and a clinician user study over three modalities found that these explanations helped clinicians verify predictions and spot likely errors. The authors' laboratory announcement states that eight clinicians' accuracy in identifying findings rose from 68.1% to 76.2%.
use_for: concept-enhanced foundation models; clinician study of concept explanations
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract; full text paywalled) + Crossref record (27 authors) + authors' laboratory news page
flags: Online-first article: no volume, issue or page numbers yet. The 68.1% to 76.2% figure and the count of eight clinicians come from the HKUST lab news page, not from the abstract or the full text, which was not accessible; verify in the paper before citing. Multi-modality model, not CT-specific.

title: Leakage and Interpretability in Concept-Based Models
key_finding: Gives an information-theoretic account of leakage in concept-based models and defines two measures: a concepts-task leakage score (unintended task information carried by the learned concepts) and an interconcept leakage score (information shared between concepts). The scores predicted how models behave under concept interventions better than existing alternatives; applied to Concept Embedding Models they revealed interconcept and alignment leakage in addition to the concepts-task leakage inherent to that design, and the paper ends with design guidelines to limit leakage.
use_for: measurement of concept leakage and its link to intervention reliability
verified_how: arXiv abstract page (v3, 24 March 2026)
flags: Preprint; the arXiv page showed no journal reference, and publication status could not be checked (search budget exhausted). General machine-learning paper, not medical imaging. Only the abstract was read.

title: Are Concept Bottleneck Models Effective as Decision-Support Systems?
key_finding: Reports two large user studies (705 participants, 6,959 observations, two binary classification tasks) testing whether concept explanations and user interventions on concepts improve human-AI team performance. CBM support, and especially the interactive intervention component, improved team accuracy over unaided humans and over non-interpretable AI support, but only when the task was perceived as hard, the concepts were easy to identify and users actually interacted with the model; inaccurate concept detection appeared to reduce trust.
use_for: empirical evidence on whether concept explanations and interventions help human decision makers
verified_how: alphaXiv page for the arXiv record (abstract)
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed. The abstract does not state the task domain or who the participants were; do not describe it as a clinician or medical-imaging study without reading the full text. arXiv primary category cs.HC.

title: Concept Bottleneck Models for Explainable Decision Making: A Survey of Progress, Taxonomy, and Future Directions
journal: Proceedings of the Thirty-Fifth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-26)
key_finding: Survey that organizes concept bottleneck research into concept acquisition, concept-based decision making, user intervention and evaluation. It traces concept construction from manual annotation through lexicon mining and generation by large language and vision-language models to visually grounded concept discovery with prototypes and diffusion models, covers designs that relax the strict bottleneck, and stresses evaluation and intervention standards based on faithfulness, sparsity and intervenability, with particular attention to healthcare.

title: Concept Bottleneck Models
journal: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Introduces the concept bottleneck model: a network first predicts human-specified concepts that are labelled at training time and then predicts the target from those concepts alone, so that a user can edit concept values at test time and see the prediction change. On x-ray grading of arthritis severity (clinical concepts) and bird identification (attribute concepts) the models were competitive with end-to-end networks, and correcting wrong concept predictions at test time improved accuracy substantially.

title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
journal: Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Defines a concept activation vector as a direction in a network's internal activation space that represents a user-chosen concept, and TCAV as a test that uses directional derivatives along that vector to quantify how much the concept influences predictions of a given class. It is demonstrated on a standard image classifier and on a medical imaging application, moving explanation from pixels to user-defined concepts.

title: Addressing Leakage in Concept Bottleneck Models
journal: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022)
key_finding: Explains that passing the concept predictor's output probabilities to the label predictor improves label accuracy but lets extra, non-concept information leak through, which lowers concept accuracy and makes test-time interventions less effective. It attributes the trade-off to an insufficient concept set and an inexpressive concept predictor, and with corresponding modifications obtains models that match the accuracy of leaky CBMs while greatly improving concept accuracy and intervention accuracy.

title: Prediction of Lobar Emphysema Progression with a CT-Based Foundational Model
key_finding: Prognostic model for COPD on serial chest CT from COPDGene and ECLIPSE (5,823 participants; foundation model trained on 2,136, tested on 2,718 internal and 969 external). The structural idea is anatomical: a foundation model learns local density patterns and a lobe-based transformer with global attention predicts the annualised change in volume-adjusted lung density for each lobe, so the output is itself a lobe-by-lobe statement. Predicted and observed lobar decline correlated modestly (mean r 0.43 internal, 0.47 external) and lobes with accelerated progression were identified with AUC about 0.70 in both test sets; the lobe-level output was validated against measured decline, but no separate evaluation of the model's attention as an explanation is described in the abstract.

TotalSegmentator outperformed MOOSE on most metrics and both outperformed LungMask, but the locally trained model was best internally and externally and handled missing lobes more reliably; public tools degraded on complex anatomy. title: LobePrior segments lung lobes on computed tomography images in the presence of severe abnormalities
key_finding: Lung-lobe segmentation method aimed at CT scans with severe parenchymal abnormality. Reported Dice was 0.966 on the LOCCA dataset and 0.978 on a COVID-19 CT dataset, with statistically significant gains over competing methods. No explanation method is evaluated; the contribution is making the anatomical partition itself robust in diseased lungs.

journal: Computer Vision – ECCV 2026 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science)

title: Evaluation of a content-based image retrieval system for radiologists in high-resolution CT of interstitial lung diseases
key_finding: Reader study of case-based reasoning in chest HRCT: a commercial similar-patient search (a ResNeXt-50 embedding trained with metric learning that maps user-drawn ROIs to a feature vector and returns ranked similar ILD cases from a database of more than 800 CTs) was tested on 28 ILD cases read by two residents and one expert. With retrieval, resident accuracy rose from 35.7% to 53.6% (not significant, p = 0.302), confidence rose from 32.2% to 50.0%, and reading time fell (104 s to 54 s, p < 0.001). The retrieved top case matched an input pattern in 73.4% of queries (77.7% with more than one ROI); here the explanation, i.e. the retrieved cases, was evaluated directly through reader performance.

title: Explaining 3D Computed Tomography Classifiers with Counterfactuals
key_finding: Extends the Latent Shift counterfactual method to whole 3D CT classifiers by using a 2D slice-wise VQ-GAN autoencoder (trained on about 1.45 million slices from 12,686 scans of LUNA16, TotalSegmentator and DeepLesion) and back-propagating the classifier gradient to only a chunk of slices at a time, which also localises where along the volume the evidence lies. Demonstrated on a lung-segmentation model (lung size) and a CT phenotype classifier for pleural effusion: on 399 PleThora/NSCLC-Radiomics volumes the mean effusion score of 77 positive scans fell from 0.24 to 0.15 for their counterfactuals (negatives 0.05). The explanation was evaluated by this prediction-reduction measure and by a single-case visual comparison with input gradients, guided backprop and Grad-CAM; the authors state that no clinical reader validation was done.

title: COGENT: Counterfactual Gaussian Explanations for Volumetric Medical Images
key_finding: Counterfactual explanation of the Sybil lung-cancer-risk model on low-dose chest CT in which the volume is re-encoded as 3D Gaussian primitives and the parameters of selected Gaussians are optimised against the frozen classifier, so the explanation is a sparse set of anatomically localised primitives rather than a voxel map. In the quantitative comparison its RRA score was 0.28 versus 0.08 for Grad-CAM and lower for saliency, integrated gradients and Kernel SHAP, with perturbation scores similar to the gradient baselines. The explanation was also graded by one radiologist on a 5-point scale (40% favourable, 40% neutral, 20% unfavourable), but the dataset and the number of cases are not reported.

title: RoentMod: a synthetic chest X-ray modification model to identify and correct image interpretation model shortcuts
key_finding: Counterfactual editing tool for chest radiographs that combines the RoentGen text-to-image generator with an image-to-image model to add a specified pathology while keeping the patient's anatomy, without retraining. In reader studies 93% of edited images looked realistic, 89-99% showed the requested finding and anatomy was preserved to a degree comparable with real follow-up films. Used as a probe, the counterfactuals showed that multi-task and foundation classifiers relied on off-target pathology as shortcuts; adding them to training raised AUC by 3-19% internally and by 1-11% for 5 of 6 pathologies externally. The counterfactuals themselves were validated by radiologist readers.

title: Predicting lung cancer survival with attention-based CT slices combination
key_finding: Two-year overall-survival prediction in non-small cell lung cancer from CT (public LUNG1, 422 patients with 7 excluded; private CLARO, 119 stage III patients). Each axial slice is encoded by a 2D EfficientNetB0, a soft attention layer weights the slices and a DeepHit head outputs risk, so the per-slice weights are the built-in explanation. The model reached a time-dependent C-index of 0.584 on LUNG1 and beat 3D baselines, but attention pooling was not significantly better than average pooling (p = 0.545). The slice attention was inspected only qualitatively (averaged weights favoured basal lung slices; one example case), with no check against annotations or faithfulness test.

title: Normal Guidance is what Attention Needs
key_finding: Tests whether attention in multiple instance learning trained with one scan-level label can localise disease at slice level on three public CT sets with held-out slice labels (RSNA head haemorrhage, RSNA pulmonary embolism chest CT with 7,279 scans and about 1.79 million slices, RSNA abdominal trauma). On chest CT plain attention-based MIL localised poorly (slice-level AUROC 0.56) and was beaten by an image-free baseline that simply puts a Gaussian at the centre of the scan (0.78); regularising the attention profile towards a bell shape ('Normal Guidance') raised it to 0.87, about equal to the paper's best-in-class reference ceiling (0.87), while scan-level AUROC stayed about 0.66-0.68. The attention-as-explanation was therefore evaluated quantitatively against slice labels, and the authors caution that it is assessed only on positive scans and may still not be a faithful account of the prediction.
use_for: (4) attention-based MIL on 3D chest CT: quantitative test of slice attention as localisation; unregularised attention can lose to a content-free baseline
