title: Probabilistic smooth attention for deep multiple instance learning in medical imaging
key_finding: Replaces deterministic MIL attention with a probability distribution over attention values that also encodes smoothness between neighbouring instances, so each slice or patch receives an attention mean and a variance. Evaluated against eleven baselines on RSNA intracranial-haemorrhage head CT (1,150 scans treated as bags of slices) and two whole-slide pathology sets; on CT the best variant reached bag AUROC 91.8 versus 91.1 for the transformer-MIL baseline, a difference within run-to-run spread. The attention and uncertainty maps are presented as the explanation but were assessed only by visual inspection; no instance-level localisation or calibration metric is reported.

title: High performance with fewer labels using semi-weakly supervised learning for pulmonary embolism diagnosis
key_finding: Asks how much slice-level annotation a 3D chest CT classifier needs: attention-based CNN-RNN models for pulmonary embolism on CT pulmonary angiography were trained on the RSPECT dataset (6,958 training exams) with exam-level labels only, all slice labels, or a fraction of slice labels, and tested externally on pooled Aida and FUMPE data (65 exams). title: Applying Conformal Prediction to a Deep Learning Model for Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection to Improve Trustworthiness
key_finding: Retrospective study on 491 non-contrast head CT volumes (CQ500) in which Mondrian (class-conditional) conformal prediction was layered on a detector that localises and classifies haemorrhage into five classes; calibration used 1,546 sections with unanimous reader labels and testing used 8,401 sections. title: Conformal Risk Control for Pulmonary Nodule Detection
journal: Proceedings of the Fourteenth Symposium on Conformal and Probabilistic Prediction with Applications (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)

title: Generalist foundation models from a multimodal dataset for 3D computed tomography
key_finding: Introduces CT-RATE, a public set of 25,692 non-contrast 3D chest CT scans from 21,304 patients, each paired with its radiology report, and uses it to train CT-CLIP (contrastive CT-report pretraining for zero-shot multi-abnormality detection and case retrieval) and CT-CHAT (CT-CLIP vision encoder plus a pretrained LLM, tuned on more than 2.7 million question-answer pairs). title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
journal: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Trains an image encoder and a text encoder from scratch on 400 million web image-caption pairs with the simple objective of matching each image to its caption (CLIP), so that class names written as text can be used for zero-shot classification. Tested on more than 30 vision datasets, it is often competitive with supervised baselines and matches ResNet-50 ImageNet accuracy zero-shot, without using any of the 1.28 million ImageNet training images. It produces image-text similarity scores only, with no built-in localisation or rationale.

title: Merlin: a computed tomography vision–language foundation model and dataset
key_finding: Merlin is a 3D vision-language model pretrained in several stages on 15,331 CT scans (over 6 million images) using two forms of existing clinical supervision, more than 1.8 million EHR diagnosis codes and over 6 million tokens of report text, with no extra manual labels. It is evaluated on 752 tasks in 6 task types (zero-shot classification of 30 findings, 692 phenotypes, image-report retrieval, 5-year prediction of 6 chronic diseases, report generation, 20-organ segmentation), with internal testing on 5,137 scans and external testing on 44,098 scans from 3 sites and 2 public datasets; the authors report it outperforms 2D vision-language models, CT foundation models and off-the-shelf radiology models, and they release 25,494 CT-report pairs from 18,317 patients. For explanation it offers text outputs (zero-shot findings, generated reports) and organ segmentation, but no finding-level grounding or rationale.
use_for: Large CT vision-language foundation model supervised by reports plus EHR codes; breadth of zero-shot and adapted tasks; example of capability without explanation

title: Large-scale and Fine-grained Vision-language Pre-training for Enhanced CT Image Understanding
key_finding: fVLM replaces whole-scan-to-whole-report contrast with anatomy-level alignment: each segmented anatomical region of a CT is matched to the report sentences describing it, with a correction for false negatives (many normal or similarly diseased samples) that moves pairing from patient-level to disease-aware. Trained on imaging and reports from 69,086 patients and tested on 54 diagnosis tasks across 15 anatomies, it reaches a mean zero-shot AUC of 81.3%, 12.9 points above CLIP and 8.0 above supervised methods, and gains 7.4 and 4.8 AUC points over prior methods on CT-RATE and Rad-ChestCT. For explanation, predictions are tied to a named organ or region (per-organ alignment), which is coarser than lesion-level grounding.
use_for: Fine-grained anatomy-level CT-report alignment; zero-shot multi-abnormality detection on chest CT benchmarks; per-organ attribution as a form of explanation

title: Towards generalist foundation model for radiology by leveraging web-scale 2D&3D medical data
key_finding: RadFM is a generative radiology model that takes interleaved text with 2D or 3D scans and answers in free text, covering diagnosis, visual question answering, report generation and rationale diagnosis. It is trained on MedMD (about 16 million scans, built from four new datasets with 13 million 2D images and 615 thousand 3D scans plus existing sets) and tuned on the cleaner RadMD subset (about 3 million samples); on the new RadBench benchmark and nine existing datasets the authors report it outperforms earlier accessible multimodal models including GPT-4V. For explanation it can output a natural-language rationale for a diagnosis, but the rationale is not grounded to image regions.
use_for: RadFM-type generalist 2D/3D radiology model; natural-language rationale as an explanation format; common baseline for CT report generation

title: Large Language Model With Region-Guided Referring and Grounding for CT Report Generation
key_finding: Reg2RG generates chest CT reports region by region: masks from a universal segmentation model (SAT) select each anatomical region, a local-feature-decoupling step keeps high-resolution texture and separate geometry cues, and a region-report alignment objective makes the LLaMA2-7B decoder first name the region and then write its findings. On RadGenome-ChestCT (25,692 region-guided CT-report pairs from 21,304 patients; 24,128 train, 1,564 test) it scores clinical-efficacy F1 0.253 against 0.212 for the best baseline and 0.139 for CT2Rep, and it is also tested on CTRG-Chest-548K (1,804 pairs). For explanation, each report passage is tied to one of 10 anatomical regions (region recognition F1 of 0.96 or higher for 8 of the 10 regions but about 0.44 for lung and pleura, which the authors attribute to the segmentation masks); the authors state it is organ-level and can miss or mislocate individual lesions.
use_for: Region-grounded (anatomy-aware) chest CT report generation; grounding as built-in interpretability and its limits at lesion level

title: CT-AGRG: Automated Abnormality-Guided Report Generation from 3D Chest CT Volumes
journal: 2025 IEEE 22nd International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI)
key_finding: CT-AGRG first classifies 18 abnormalities on a chest CT volume and then has a biomedical GPT-2 write one sentence for each abnormality predicted present, instead of generating the whole report in one pass. On CT-RATE (the paper reports 17,799 training patients and a test set of 1,314 patients / 3,039 volumes) the CT-Net variant raises clinical-efficacy F1 from 36.73 (CT2Rep) to 50.11 and recall from 38.12 to 62.59. For explanation, each generated sentence is traceable to a named predicted abnormality, which gives control over content, but there is no spatial localisation.

title: RadGPT: Constructing 3D Image-Text Tumor Datasets
journal: 2025 IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
key_finding: RadGPT converts tumour and organ segmentation masks into structured and narrative reports (size, location, attenuation, resectability), and was used with 12 board-certified radiologists to build AbdomenAtlas 3.0: 9,262 CT/mask/report triplets (3,955 with liver, kidney or pancreatic tumours) drawn from 17 public datasets, with 3,011 newly identified tumour cases. Run fully automatically it acts as a segmentation-assisted report generator; benchmarked against 5 report-generation vision-language models, the authors report that the segmentation step strongly improves tumour detection in generated reports. For explanation, every reported finding is backed by a per-voxel mask, i.e. the report is grounded by construction.

title: Development of a large-scale grounded vision language dataset for chest CT analysis
key_finding: RadGenome-Chest CT extends CT-RATE (25,692 chest CT volumes, 21,304 patients) with organ-level segmentation masks for 197 categories, 665 thousand multi-granularity grounded reports in which each sentence is linked to a segmented anatomical region, and 1.2 million grounded question-answer pairs whose questions and answers point to reference masks. It was built automatically with a universal segmentation model (SAT) and large language models. For explanation, it is the training resource that lets a model generate text for a given region and tie each statement to visual evidence.

title: 3D-RAD: A Comprehensive 3D Radiology Med-VQA Dataset with Multi-Temporal Analysis and Diverse Diagnostic Tasks
journal: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
key_finding: 3D-RAD is a visual question answering dataset built on CT-RATE chest CT (16,188 scans from 11,255 patients; about 170 thousand QA pairs, of which 33,910 form the benchmark and 136,195 the training set) with six tasks: anomaly detection, image observation, medical computation, existence detection, and static and longitudinal temporal diagnosis. Existing 3D medical vision-language models generalise poorly zero-shot, especially on the temporal tasks, and fine-tuning M3D on the training set lifts existence-detection accuracy from 18.0% to 81.1% (Llama2-7B variant). For explanation, answers are short free text (type, feature, location, size of a finding) with no region mask, and QA pairs were LLM-generated from reports with a 91% human agreement check on a 600-pair sample.

title: ReXGroundingCT: A 3D Chest CT Dataset for Segmentation of Findings from Free-Text Reports
key_finding: ReXGroundingCT links free-text findings to 3D segmentations on 3,142 non-contrast chest CT scans from CT-RATE: 8,028 text-to-segmentation pairs covering 16,301 annotated entities, about 79% focal and 21% non-focal lung and pleural abnormalities. Findings were extracted and standardised with GPT-4 and categorised with GPT-4o-mini; training masks were quality-assured by radiologists, and the 50-case public validation set and 100-case private test set were fully annotated by board-certified radiologists, with a public leaderboard. For explanation, it is a benchmark for whether a model can point, at voxel level, to the region that supports a specific report sentence.

title: CT-FineBench: A Diagnostic Fidelity Benchmark for Fine-Grained Evaluation of CT Report Generation
key_finding: CT-FineBench scores a generated CT report by question answering: clinical attributes of each finding (such as location, size and margin) are turned into QA pairs grounded in the reference reports of CT-RATE and Merlin, the questions are then asked of the generated report, and answer correctness gives the score. The authors report better agreement with expert clinical assessment than earlier lexical or entity-matching metrics and much higher sensitivity to fine-grained factual errors. For explanation, it shows where a generated report is factually wrong at attribute level, which standard overlap metrics hide.

title: Comparative evaluation of generative AI models for chest radiograph report generation in the emergency department
key_finding: In 478 emergency-department adults who had chest radiography and CT on the same day, three thoracic radiologists blindly rated reports from five vision-language models (AIRead, Lingshu, MAIRA-2, MedGemma, MedVersa) and from radiologists for RADPEER agreement, clinical acceptability, hallucination and clarity, with CT as the reference for finding-level accuracy. One model (AIRead) had fewer significant discrepancies than radiologist reports (RADPEER 3b 5.3% vs 13.9%), higher acceptability (84.5% vs 74.3%) and a hallucination rate not different from radiologists (0.3% vs 0.1%), while the other four hallucinated in 5.4% to 17.4% of reports and sensitivity for common findings varied widely. For explanation, it shows that fluent generated text can be clearer than human text yet still contain unsupported findings at model-dependent rates.
use_for: Radiologist-rated hallucination and factual-error rates of report-generating vision-language models, with CT as reference standard

title: Evaluating Reasoning Faithfulness in Medical Vision-Language Models using Multimodal Perturbations
journal: Proceedings of the Fifth Machine Learning for Health Symposium (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Proposes a perturbation test of chain-of-thought explanations in chest radiograph VQA: text and image cues are deliberately injected or altered and the explanation is scored on clinical fidelity, causal attribution (does it acknowledge what actually changed the answer) and confidence calibration. Across six vision-language models, answer accuracy and explanation quality diverged, mentioning an injected cue did not mean the reasoning was grounded in it, and text cues moved explanations more than image cues; proprietary models attributed far more often than open-source ones (25.0% vs 1.4%). An automated evaluator agreed with radiologists within the inter-radiologist range in a 4-reader study (Kendall tau-b 0.670 for attribution, 0.387 for fidelity, 0.091 for confidence tone). Implication: fluent step-by-step rationales from these models are often not faithful to how the answer was reached.
use_for: Direct evidence that natural-language rationales from medical vision-language models can be unfaithful; method for testing faithfulness

title: Determinants of Reader-LLM Interaction in Thoracic Radiology: Impact of Model Confidence and Reader Expertise
key_finding: Ten readers interpreted 100 thoracic cases (radiography, CT, MRI, PET) unaided and then with LLM advice consisting of five ranked diagnoses with confidence scores and written rationales, randomised per reader-case to a high-accuracy model (GPT-5, 76% correct) or a low-accuracy model (GPT-4o, 27%). Appropriate use of the advice (accepting correct, rejecting incorrect suggestions) was associated with model confidence (OR 3.82) and reader expertise (OR 2.06). Better-rated rationales reduced rejection of correct suggestions (OR 0.79) but increased acceptance of incorrect ones (OR 1.71). Implication: persuasive text rationales raise overreliance, so a higher-quality rationale is not a safeguard against wrong advice.
use_for: Whether LLM text rationales help or mislead radiologists in thoracic imaging; overreliance and automation bias
verified_how: RSNA landing page (abstract, online date, volume, issue) + Crossref record (15 authors, article number)

title: The effect of medical explanations from large language models on diagnostic accuracy in radiology
key_finding: A randomised between-subjects vignette experiment with 101 US radiologists (2,020 free-text diagnoses on 20 published image-challenge cases with CT or MRI) compared no LLM support against three GPT-4 output formats: diagnosis only, a five-item differential, and a chain-of-thought explanation. Chain-of-thought output gave the highest accuracy, 12.2 points above control (P = 0.001), 7.2 above diagnosis-only and 9.7 above the differential format, and the effect held across case difficulty and radiologist specialisation. Implication: the format of a text explanation changes clinician accuracy, and stepwise reasoning helped readers spot wrong LLM answers in this setting.
use_for: Evidence that natural-language reasoning explanations can help radiologists; counterpoint to overreliance findings

title: Evaluating Explainability: A Framework for Systematic Assessment of Explainable AI Features in Medical Imaging
key_finding: Authors from the US FDA device centre propose a staged framework for testing heatmap-type explanations of imaging AI on four criteria: consistency (stability under small input changes, scored with SSIM, MSE or IoU), plausibility (overlap with lesion ground truth), fidelity (model-parameter randomisation and incremental deletion) and usefulness (human reader studies), plus an 'explainability card' for reporting. In a case study with 150 synthetic mammograms (M-SYNTH) and a Faster R-CNN detector, Ablation-CAM scored higher than Eigen-CAM on plausibility and fidelity, while both maps fluctuated under dose and rotation changes that left detection accuracy stable. Usefulness was not tested, no acceptance thresholds are set, and exact metric values are given only in figures.

title: Evaluating the robustness of explainable AI in medical image recognition under natural and adversarial data corruption
key_finding: Benchmarks the stability of ten post-hoc explanation methods (eight for CNNs including Integrated Gradients, SmoothGrad, Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++; AttnLRP and LibraGrad for transformers) on eight classifiers across three MedMNIST sets (dermatoscopy, paediatric chest radiographs with 5,856 images, retinal OCT), under natural corruptions (contrast reduction, JPEG compression, speckle noise) and an adversarial attack that alters the explanation while keeping the predicted class. Stability is scored with L2 distance, SSIM and a new spatial metric (Convolution Density Agreement); 160 configurations per data set. Many methods changed under imperceptible perturbations and no method was best on every metric: SmoothGrad was most stable against the attack and Grad-CAM++ against natural noise for CNNs.

title: More than just a heatmap: elevating XAI with rigorous evaluation metrics
key_finding: Introduces XAlign, a single composite score for how well a saliency map matches expert tumour annotations, built from three terms: concentration of attribution inside the lesion, adherence to the lesion boundary, and a penalty for scattered attribution. It is applied to compare Grad-CAM, LIME, SHAP and the native saliency of the authors' own CNN-spiking hybrid classifier (SpikeNet) on TCGA-LGG brain MRI (22-fold patient-level cross-validation) and BUSI breast ultrasound (5-fold); the native maps scored highest on both data sets. The component weights were fixed on a held-out dermoscopy set (ISIC 2019) and not tuned per data set.
use_for: 1 (also 2) - example of a composite/unified explanation-quality index (plausibility type, mask based) and of post-hoc methods being ranked head-to-head on MRI

title: XIMED: A Dual-Loop Evaluation Framework Integrating Predictive Model and Human-Centered Approaches for Explainable AI in Medical Imaging
key_finding: Proposes a two-part evaluation of explanation methods for chest radiograph classification and applies it to LIME and SHAP. The model-centred loop checks whether explanations respond as expected to changes in model inputs, outputs and internal structure; the human-centred loop is a study with 97 medical experts who rated trust, confidence and agreement with supporting and opposing evidence before and after seeing explanations. Both methods reacted to model changes; SHAP had more influence on diagnostic changes and helped correct wrong initial diagnoses, and explanations raised trust and agreement when the clinician's first diagnosis was correct.

title: Attention Without Grounding: Causal Evaluation of Visual Explanations in Medical VLMs
key_finding: Audits heatmap explanations of chest radiograph vision-language models (three MedGemma-4B variants, LLaVA-RAD, Qwen3-VL, CheXagent) on three axes: overlap with radiologist boxes on PadChest (n=637), pointing game, attribution mass in mask and pixel-AP against radiologist masks on CheXlocalize (n=643), and patch-occlusion causal maps with insertion/deletion curves. Six attribution methods are compared (raw attention, attention rollout, gradient x attention, Winsor-CAM, integrated gradients, RISE). No vision-language model passed: none placed more than 22% of attribution inside the radiologist mask and attention was negatively correlated with causal importance (Spearman rho -0.05 to -0.17), whereas Grad-CAM on two chest-radiograph CNN classifiers passed the same protocol (p<1e-4 versus shuffled maps).

title: Faithful Faithfulness Evaluations: Challenges & Pitfalls Learned from a Breast MRI Case Study
key_finding: Compares seven saliency methods (last-layer attention, attention rollout, Grad-SAM, gradient attention rollout, GMAR, Grad-CAM, HiResCAM) for a transformer classifier of 3D breast MRI (ODELIA challenge data, 1,022 unilateral breast volumes, 116 in the test set) using deletion and insertion curves summarised as area under the confidence curve. Method rankings changed with the masking strategy (black, white, minimum intensity, attention masking); with fixed-intensity masking most methods were close to random ordering. Grad-CAM and gradient attention rollout were the strongest class-specific methods (deletion AUCC 0.336 each versus 0.512 for random), but their order depended on the protocol, and the advantage shrank when class-agnostic variants were compared.

title: Decision processes in 3D structural MRI schizophrenia classification evaluated with saliency maps
key_finding: Trained seven 3D deep learning architectures (two from scratch, five pretrained) to separate schizophrenia from controls on T1-weighted MRI of 192 adults (101 patients, 91 controls; MCIC collection) and examined each with Grad-CAM. Plausibility was judged visually and with two quantitative measures: share of saliency mass inside the brain, and centre-of-mass deviation and spread. All models reached similar accuracy (above 70%, AUC above 0.75, no significant differences), yet only two of the seven (BrainID and ResNet18) based their decisions on plausible brain structure.

title: Evaluating cognitive biases in AI-assisted mammography interpretation: a simulation reader study of explainable AI across radiologist experience levels
key_finding: Single-centre, fully crossed simulation study: six breast radiologists of three experience levels read 200 mammograms unaided, with AI, and with AI plus saliency heatmaps; the AI's BI-RADS-like recommendation was deliberately shifted by one category in 30% of examinations. Without heatmaps, automation bias occurred in 65/180 (36.1%) and anchoring-related revision in 61/180 (33.9%) manipulated readings; with heatmaps these fell to 32/180 (17.8%) and 31/180 (17.2%) (adjusted odds ratios 0.56 and 0.61, both p<0.001). On unmanipulated cases accuracy rose from 86.2% unaided to 90.1% with AI plus heatmaps; less experienced readers were most affected and the bias was reduced but not removed.

title: Automation Bias in Action: Eye Tracking of Humans Reading Screening Mammograms with and without AI Prompts
key_finding: Retrospective paired multireader study with eye tracking: 10 readers from the UK breast screening programme read 60 two-view screening mammograms unaided and, six weeks later, with a commercial AI tool that displayed region prompts (26 true-positive, 14 false-negative, 14 false-positive, 6 true-negative AI outputs). For cancers the AI missed, median reader sensitivity fell from 71% unaided to 39% with AI (P=.002); for false-positive AI cases median specificity rose from 21% to 39% (P=.004). Reading time rose with the number of prompts (median 25 s with none to 34 s with four or more) and fixation rate on missed cancers was lower with AI.

title: The impact of AI feedback on the accuracy of diagnosis, decision switching and trust in radiography
key_finding: Online experiment with 94 participants (54 student and 40 qualified radiographers) who each judged three upper-limb radiographic examinations before AI feedback, after a Grad-CAM-style heatmap, and after a binary AI diagnosis with a percentage confidence. The ResNet-152 model was correct on only 12 of the 21 examinations used. Feedback improved accuracy when the AI was right but accuracy fell when it was wrong (by 9.6% for students and 4.3% for radiographers); in abnormal cases the heatmap alone lowered accuracy (65.85% to 57.62%) before the binary output raised it to 72.35%. Students switched decisions more often than radiographers (23.5% vs 14.3% after the heatmap) and self-reported trust dropped by 0.7 points on a 5-point scale in both groups.
use_for: 3 - comparison of two feedback forms (heatmap versus label with confidence) on accuracy, decision switching and trust; shows a heatmap alone can mislead less experienced readers
verified_how: PLOS ONE article page (abstract and full text read) + Ulster University repository record
flags: Readers are radiographers and students, not radiologists; musculoskeletal radiographs; convenience sample; each participant saw only three examinations. Sixth author is spelled 'Devinder Kumar' on the journal page and 'Deviner Kumar' in the repository record; the journal spelling is used.

title: Eye-Tracking Evidence That Verifiable Explanations Support Visual Evidence Checking in AI-Assisted Chest Radiograph Interpretation
key_finding: A 2x2 between-subjects eye-tracking experiment (verifiable explanation present or absent; high or low risk context) with 56 clinically trained participants (clerkship students, residents, attending physicians; 14 per cell), each completing 24 pleural-effusion decisions on chest radiographs with AI advice that was wrong in 6 trials. Outcomes were gaze switches between the AI output and the image and dwell time on the image. Explanations did not simply raise acceptance: when the AI was wrong, participants with explanations switched between AI output and image more often (about 8.5 vs 6.0 per trial) and looked at the image longer (about 5.1 s vs 4.3 s).
use_for: 3 - process-level (gaze) evidence that explanations which can be checked against the image promote verification of wrong AI advice on chest radiographs
verified_how: MDPI article page (abstract and most of the full text read)
flags: Small cells (14 per condition), mixed training levels, one binary task with fixed case-correctness pairing. Authors present the gaze measures as markers of checking, not proof of better diagnosis. Chest radiographs, not CT.

title: Dermatologist-like explainable AI enhances melanoma diagnosis accuracy: eye-tracking study
key_finding: Reader study with eye tracking in which 76 dermatologists each diagnosed 16 dermoscopic images of melanomas and naevi, first with a plain AI prediction and then with an explainable AI giving domain-specific explanations. Mean balanced accuracy rose from 79.9% with AI to 82.7% with explainable AI (gain 2.8 percentage points, P=0.013). Disagreement with the classifier and difficult lesions were associated with more fixations, read by the authors as higher cognitive load; the accuracy gain was unrelated to years of experience and trust was not measured in this study.
use_for: 3 - non-radiology comparator showing a small but significant accuracy gain from concept-style explanations over AI alone, with gaze data on cognitive load
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract and results read) + Crossref record for the author list
flags: Dermoscopy, not radiology. Byline has 20 named authors, the Reader Study Consortium and the senior author; Crossref also lists about 80 consortium members as individual authors, which are not reproduced here. Fixed order (AI first, then explainable AI) rather than randomised arms; the gain was significant in the webcam cohort (n=51) but not in the device-based cohort (n=25).

title: Exploring Radiologists' Expectations of Explainable Machine Learning Models in Medical Image Analysis
url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11700 ; https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2604.11700 (PDF text read through alphaXiv)
key_finding: A 30-question structured survey of 46 respondents (26 radiologists and 20 radiology residents) from the hospitals of one university, most working with CT and MRI. Explainability was called a prerequisite for trust by 42 of 46. The elements most often named as making a model explainable were reliance on clinically relevant imaging features (residents 70%, senior radiologists 86%) and visual heatmaps (65% and 79%); 86% of senior radiologists but no residents wanted standardised radiological scoring systems, and counterfactual explanations were least selected (33%). When model and reader disagree most would examine the explanation before deciding; respondents ranked task performance, then model confidence, then explanation quality when judging outputs, and 78% and 74% asked for external and prospective validation.
use_for: 3 - survey evidence on what radiologists say they want from explanations (relevant features, heatmaps, scoring-system terms, confidence) and how wishes differ by seniority
verified_how: arXiv abstract page + alphaXiv full text of arXiv:2604.11700v1
flags: PREPRINT, not peer reviewed (text says data will be released on acceptance). Single-institution convenience sample; stated preferences, not measured performance. Ethics approval details withheld in the preprint. No published version found by web search on 2026-10-10.

title: Mask of Truth: Model Sensitivity to Unexpected Regions of Medical Images
journal: Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine
key_finding: Tests for shortcut learning by training DenseNet-121 classifiers on chest radiographs with the lungs removed or kept (PadChest, 93,203 images after filtering, five findings; external test on 22,004 ChestX-ray14 images) and on fundus images (Chaksu). Chest models stayed well above chance with the lungs masked out by a bounding box (effusion AUC 0.85-0.93, pneumonia at least 0.74) and above metadata-only baselines, while lung-only images gave AUCs near 0.5 for several findings. SHAP maps pointed to a pacemaker for cardiomegaly and to peripheral image areas; a radiology resident identified only 2 of 35 present conditions on the masked images, and external performance was far lower than internal.
use_for: 4 - masking experiment plus SHAP showing chest radiograph classifiers can perform without the clinically relevant region; also notes that local attribution maps can miss global shortcuts
verified_how: Springer article page (abstract and full text read) + Crossref record
flags: Chest radiographs and fundus, not CT. Online first 20 May 2025; assigned to volume 39 issue 1 (February 2026). Springer page truncated the byline; the five-author list is from Crossref. Crossref short title is recorded as shown.

title: Explainable AI reveals Clever Hans effects in unsupervised learning models
key_finding: Uses explanation methods to show that unsupervised representation-learning and anomaly-detection models, including foundation models, often predict correctly for the wrong reasons. In the medical example a COVID-19 detector built on PubMedCLIP features (2,597 NIH CXR8 radiographs plus 535 images from a public COVID-19 collection) reached 87.5% class-balanced accuracy overall but only 81.7% with a 51% false-positive rate on the COVID-source subset; BiLRP explanations traced this to text-like annotations on the images. The authors attribute the effect largely to inductive biases of the unsupervised learner and report that targeted mitigation improved robustness.
use_for: 4 - Clever Hans effect inherited from a pretrained medical foundation model and exposed by explanations in a chest radiograph task; relevant to foundation-model-based chest CT pipelines
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract and results read) + Crossref record for the author list
flags: The chest radiograph experiment is one of several use cases; most of the paper is general machine learning. Chest radiographs, not CT.

title: Uncertainty-Driven Training for Three-Dimensional Calibrated Lung Nodule Classification
journal: Artificial Neural Networks and Machine Learning - ICANN 2026 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 17092)
key_finding: Proposes a training scheme for 3D CT lung nodule classifiers in which validation-set uncertainty estimates reweight the loss towards unreliable classes, comparing Monte Carlo dropout with evidential deep learning on five backbones (ResNet, DenseNet, EfficientNet, ViT, Swin) using LIDC-IDRI and NoduleMNIST3D. Classification performance stayed similar to standard training while expected calibration error fell by up to 65% on LIDC-IDRI; gains were more consistent for convolutional than transformer backbones, evidential learning degraded on ViT, and simple post-hoc temperature scaling was highly effective in every configuration.
use_for: 5 - chest CT evidence that nodule classifiers are miscalibrated by default and that calibration (expected calibration error) should be reported alongside accuracy; temperature scaling as a strong baseline
verified_how: Springer chapter page (abstract; full text behind preview) + arXiv abstract page 2609.20905
flags: Conference paper (ICANN 2026). Springer shows first online 14 September 2026 but a 2027 copyright/citation year; year is recorded as 2027 with the 2026 online date, so it counts as 2026 under the online-first rule. Only the abstract was read, which gives a single number (up to 65% ECE reduction); absolute ECE values and nodule counts are not recorded. No explanation method or reader study is involved.

title: Human-AI Collaboration in Radiology: The Blind Spots
key_finding: Special report (narrative synthesis, no new data) arguing that radiology AI research has concentrated on stand-alone algorithm performance while the human-AI interaction that determines clinical value is poorly understood. It sets out three under-recognised determinants: cognitive psychology (automation bias, how AI uncertainty is framed, AI-induced skill decay), interface and user-experience design (timing, prominence and documentation of AI findings), and algorithmic conformity driven by medicolegal, transparency and organisational pressure; research directions are proposed for each.
use_for: 5 (also 3) - peer-reviewed synthesis linking how AI output and uncertainty are presented to automation bias and reliance; frames explanation and confidence display as interface-design questions
verified_how: RSNA article page (abstract read; full text paywalled)
flags: Narrative special report, not a systematic review; only the abstract was read. Article e-number not shown on the page (pages left null). Not specific to chest CT.

title: Explainability and AI Confidence in Clinical Decision Support Systems: Effects on Trust, Diagnostic Performance, and Cognitive Load in Breast Cancer Care
key_finding: Web-based interrupted time-series experiment with 28 US clinicians (about 60% radiologists) who diagnosed breast ultrasound images under five successive conditions: no AI, AI label, label with class probabilities, added tumour localisation, and localisation with high- and low-confidence regions (10 images per condition; AI accuracy 81%). In the preprint analysis, low AI confidence lowered trust and agreement and lengthened decisions, whereas high confidence was associated with a small but significant drop in diagnostic performance, interpreted as over-reliance; adding localisation with probabilities significantly increased reported stress, and mental demand did not change significantly.
use_for: 5 (also 3) - evidence that displaying AI confidence changes reliance in both directions: low confidence prompts caution, high confidence invites over-reliance
verified_how: Crossref record (bibliographic data) + Stevens Institute repository record (abstract) + arXiv preprint 2501.16693 read through alphaXiv (methods and results)
flags: Publisher page (tandfonline) could not be opened; the journal abstract was read on the institutional repository page and details come from the arXiv version via an alphaXiv machine-generated report, so numbers may differ from the final article. The repository abstract says high confidence raised trust, while the preprint report gives that effect as not significant. Breast ultrasound, 28 participants, no control arm, condition order not randomised. Crossref prints the journal name with an en dash.

title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
journal: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31 (NeurIPS 2018)
key_finding: Introduces randomisation tests for saliency methods: an explanation should change when the trained model's parameters or the training labels are randomised. Several popular methods produced maps that were largely independent of both the model and the data-generating process, behaving like edge detectors, so visual appeal alone is a misleading criterion; theory for a linear model and a one-layer convolutional network supports the experiments.
use_for: 1 - original source of the model- and data-randomisation sanity checks
verified_how: NeurIPS proceedings abstract page
flags: Essential original (2018). Page range and DOI not shown on the page opened. Methods and data sets are not named in the abstract and are not recorded.

title: Evaluating the Visualization of What a Deep Neural Network Has Learned
journal: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
journal_abbrev: IEEE Trans. Neural Netw. Learning Syst.
key_finding: Proposes region perturbation as an objective test of heatmaps: image regions are perturbed in order of assigned relevance (most relevant first) and the drop in the classifier score is summarised as the area over the perturbation curve (AOPC). On SUN397, ILSVRC2012 and MIT Places (5,040 images each), layer-wise relevance propagation gave larger AOPC and less complex heatmaps than sensitivity maps or deconvolution; the paper also shows that the outcome depends on how regions are perturbed.
use_for: 1 - original definition of perturbation-curve (deletion-type) faithfulness evaluation and the AOPC score
verified_how: Crossref record (bibliographic data) + arXiv:1509.06321v1 full text (abstract and method)
flags: Essential original (2017). Abstract was read in the arXiv version, where the fourth author appears as Sebastian Bach; Crossref lists him as Lapuschkin. Crossref gives the DOI in lower case and no online date. Natural images only.

title: Assessing the Trustworthiness of Saliency Maps for Localizing Abnormalities in Medical Imaging
key_finding: Evaluated eight saliency methods (gradient, SmoothGrad, integrated gradients, smooth integrated gradients, Grad-CAM, XRAI, guided backpropagation, guided Grad-CAM) on chest radiograph classifiers using the SIIM-ACR pneumothorax set (10,675 images) and the RSNA pneumonia set (14,863 images), against four criteria: localisation utility, sensitivity to weight randomisation, repeatability and reproducibility, scored with AUPRC and SSIM. Every method failed at least one criterion and all localised worse than dedicated networks (AUPRC 0.024-0.224 versus 0.404 for U-Net in segmentation; 0.160-0.519 versus 0.596 for RetinaNet in detection).
use_for: 1 and 2 - reference multi-criterion benchmark of saliency maps on chest radiographs; template for the criteria a chest CT evaluation should cover
verified_how: RSNA article page (abstract read) + arXiv listing 2008.02766 for the full author list
flags: Essential original (2021). RSNA page hides middle authors behind 'Show All'; the 13 names visible there match the 13-author arXiv listing, which was used to confirm the list (Crossref record could not be opened). The arXiv version carries a slightly different title ('(Un)Trustworthiness'). Article e-number not shown.

title: Quantus: An Explainable AI Toolkit for Responsible Evaluation of Neural Network Explanations and Beyond
key_finding: Software paper presenting Quantus, an open-source Python toolkit that gathers a growing collection of tested metrics for evaluating explanations of neural network predictions, with tutorials, distributed through PyPI and GitHub; motivated by the absence of a tool for systematic and reproducible evaluation of explanation methods.
use_for: 1 - toolkit reference for computing faithfulness, robustness, localisation, complexity and randomisation metrics
verified_how: JMLR paper page (abstract read)
flags: Essential original (2023). No DOI shown on the JMLR page. The abstract does not list the metric categories; the category names in use_for are the reviewer's shorthand and should be checked against the paper before being attributed to it.

title: Towards Faithfully Interpretable NLP Systems: How Should We Define and Evaluate Faithfulness?
journal: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
key_finding: Position paper arguing that the criteria for judging an interpretation should be kept apart and that faithfulness, meaning how accurately an explanation reflects the model's actual reasoning, deserves separate treatment. It groups existing faithfulness evaluations under three assumptions, gives guidance on how interpretation methods should and should not be tested, and proposes replacing the yes/no notion of faithfulness with a graded one.
use_for: 1 - conceptual source for separating faithfulness from plausibility when classifying evaluation metrics
verified_how: ACL Anthology page (abstract read)
flags: Essential original (2020). Natural language processing, not imaging. The word 'plausibility' does not appear in the abstract summary read; the faithfulness-versus-plausibility contrast is developed in the paper body, which was not opened.

title: AI for radiographic COVID-19 detection selects shortcuts over signal
key_finding: Shows with explanation methods that deep learning systems detecting COVID-19 on chest radiographs relied on confounders such as laterality markers, text annotations and patient positioning rather than disease signs; performance fell at new hospitals. The cause is traced to data sets that combine positives and negatives from different sources, a practice the authors note is also used for CT; external testing alone did not reliably reveal the problem, so explanation-based auditing is recommended before deployment.
use_for: 4 - landmark demonstration of shortcut learning in chest imaging uncovered through explanations
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract read)
flags: Essential original (2021). Chest radiographs; the remark on CT concerns data-collection practice, not a CT experiment.

title: Do as AI say: susceptibility in deployment of clinical decision-aids
key_finding: Experiment in which 138 radiologists and 127 internal or emergency medicine physicians each reviewed eight chest radiograph cases with diagnostic advice that was sometimes wrong and was labelled as coming from an AI or from an experienced radiologist (all advice was written by human experts). Radiologists rated AI-labelled advice as lower quality, the other group did not; diagnostic accuracy was significantly worse with inaccurate advice whatever its stated source, and 27.5% of radiologists and 41.7% of the other physicians always followed incorrect advice.
use_for: 3 - baseline evidence of over-reliance on incorrect advice in chest radiograph reading, independent of whether the source is labelled AI
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract and results read)
flags: Essential original (2021). Percentages are from the results section as summarised from the page, not the abstract. Advice was text without visual explanation.

title: Global cancer statistics 2022: GLOBOCAN estimates of incidence and mortality worldwide for 36 cancers in 185 countries
journal: CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians
key_finding: IARC GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates give close to 20 million new cancer cases and 9.7 million cancer deaths worldwide in 2022. Lung cancer was the most frequently diagnosed cancer (almost 2.5 million new cases, 12.4% of all cancers) and the leading cause of cancer death (about 1.8 million deaths, 18.7% of cancer deaths), ahead of female breast (11.6% of cases) and colorectal cancer (9.6% of cases; 9.3% of deaths). New cases are projected to reach 35 million by 2050 on demographic change alone.
use_for: Introduction: global lung cancer burden as the clinical motivation for chest CT AI
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata + abstract field)
flags: Published 2024 (allowed by task as the latest GLOBOCAN statistics paper). Publisher (Wiley) page not opened; numbers taken from the abstract deposited in Crossref.

title: Low-dose CT for lung cancer screening in a high-risk population (SUMMIT): a prospective, longitudinal cohort study
key_finding: Prospective London cohort (329 primary care practices) of 12,773 high-risk people aged 55-77 screened with low-dose CT; this report covers the baseline round. Lung cancer was diagnosed in 261 participants (2.0%), 79.3% at stage I or II and 77.0% treated by surgical resection; 12-month episode sensitivity was 97.0% and specificity 95.2% (false-positive rate 4.8%), with 11.6% of surgical resections benign. The authors conclude that large-scale LDCT screening can be delivered effectively to an ethnically and socioeconomically diverse population.
use_for: Introduction: recent prospective evidence that LDCT lung cancer screening works at scale (drives chest CT volume)
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + UCL Discovery repository record (abstract)
flags: Author list: Crossref gives 139 author entries (named writing group followed by SUMMIT consortium members, with repeats); the 36 names listed here are the first block before names start repeating and are taken to be the byline, published on behalf of the SUMMIT consortium - check against the journal PDF. Crossref shows an erratum (DOI 10.1016/S1470-2045(25)00204-9, May 2025) whose content I did not read. Online-first date not shown. Lancet website could not be opened. Funded by GRAIL.

title: Feasibility of AI as first reader in the 4-IN-THE-LUNG-RUN lung cancer screening trial: impact on negative-misclassifications and clinical referral rate
key_finding: On 3,678 baseline low-dose CT scans from the 4-IN-THE-LUNG-RUN trial, a commercial AI system (AVIEW-LCS) and radiologists read independently against an expert-panel reference. AI produced 31 negative misclassifications (0.8%) versus 407 (11.1%) for radiologists; used as first reader, AI would have missed 3 of 102 referrals (2.9%) compared with 12 of 102 (11.8%) for radiologists. The authors conclude AI is a feasible first reader to rule out negative baseline scans.
use_for: Clinical context: AI as an autonomous or first reader in CT screening, which raises the stakes for explanation and oversight
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + Erasmus University repository record (abstract)
flags: Crossref lists a corrigendum (DOI 10.1016/j.ejca.2025.115294, Eur J Cancer vol 218, March 2025); I could not read what it corrects, so re-check the numbers against the corrected version. ScienceDirect page not opened. Issue number not assigned (volume 216, article 115214).

title: Projected US Imaging Utilization, 2025 to 2055
journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
key_finding: Using 2018-2022 claims (Medicare fee-for-service 5% sample plus the Inovalon database; 348,214,053 person-years), the authors project US imaging use to 2055. If current per-person use simply persists, 2055 utilisation is 16.9% to 26.9% above 2023 levels depending on modality; if recent trends continue to 2030 the range is 5.6% lower to 45.2% higher. Population growth explains 73-88% of the increase and ageing 12-27%.
use_for: Introduction: growth in imaging demand and radiologist workload as a driver for AI assistance
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + Ochsner institutional repository record (abstract)
flags: Covers all imaging modalities in the US, not chest CT specifically. Journal abbreviation 'J Am Coll Radiol' seen on the repository page (Crossref short title is the full name). Online-first date not shown. ScienceDirect page not opened.

title: External Test of a Deep Learning Algorithm for Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy Risk Stratification Using European Screening Data
key_finding: A nodule malignancy-risk deep learning model trained on NLST was tested retrospectively on pooled baseline scans from three European screening trials (DLCST, MILD, NELSON): 4,146 participants, 7,614 benign and 180 malignant nodules. AUCs were 0.98, 0.96 and 0.94 for cancers diagnosed within 1 year, 2 years and over the whole screening period, at least matching the PanCan model; for indeterminate 5-15 mm nodules, at 100% sensitivity for 1-year cancers, the model labelled 68.1% of benign cases low risk versus 47.4% for PanCan (a 39.4% relative reduction in false positives). On a size-matched subset the AUC was 0.79 versus 0.60.
use_for: Performance of deep learning on chest CT: large multi-trial external validation (2025)
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page + UMC Utrecht repository record (abstract)
flags: Byline ends 'for the NELSON-POP consortium'; Crossref additionally lists the consortium members as authors (not included here). Retrospective design.

title: External Testing of a Deep Learning Model for Lung Cancer Risk from Low-Dose Chest CT
key_finding: The open-source Sybil lung-cancer-risk model was tested on 18,057 adults aged 50-80 from one Asian health-checkup centre (92 cancers over 6 years). Overall AUC was 0.91 for 1-year and 0.74 for 6-year risk; in heavy smokers the 1-year AUC for visible cancers was 0.94 and the 6-year AUC for future cancers 0.70, but in never- or light-smokers the AUC for future cancers fell to 0.56 (visible cancers 0.89). The model therefore transfers poorly to a population outside its training distribution for the task of predicting future cancer.
use_for: Generalisation limits of chest CT deep learning across populations (motivates transparency about where a model can be trusted)
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page + Jeonbuk National University repository record (abstract)
flags: Single-centre retrospective external test; the generalisation gap is across population/smoking status rather than across scanners.

title: Artificial intelligence as an independent reader of risk-dominant lung nodules: influence of CT reconstruction parameters
key_finding: Baseline low-dose CT scans of 300 consecutive NELCIN-B3 screening participants (Tianjin) were read by a commercial AI system under four reconstruction settings, with two-radiologist consensus as reference. Per-scan sensitivity for a risk-dominant nodule was 77.5% with the medium-soft D45f/1 mm kernel but 31.5% with the sharp B80f/1 mm kernel (p<0.0001), and nodule-type agreement dropped from 87.7% to 17.7%, while the nodule detection rate itself (87.4% vs 82.0%) and a change from 1 mm to 2 mm slices made no significant difference. A single acquisition parameter can thus sharply change the output of a deployed AI reader.
use_for: Generalisation failure of commercial chest CT AI across reconstruction settings (2025-2026 evidence)
verified_how: Springer landing page (abstract) + Crossref record
flags: Issue year 2026 (vol 36, issue 3, March 2026); first online 29 Aug 2025. Two co-authors (Yu D, Yi J) are likely vendor-affiliated - affiliations not checked.

title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
key_finding: Consensus guideline from 117 experts in 50 countries setting out 30 best practices under six principles: fairness, universality, traceability, usability, robustness and explainability. Explainability has two recommendations: decide with end users and domain experts whether explanations are needed and define their goal, approach and limitations; and evaluate explanations both computationally for correctness and with end users for their effect on satisfaction, confidence and clinical performance. Traceability has six (risk management file, documentation, continuous quality control with calibrated uncertainty, periodic auditing and updating, AI logging, and governance with defined accountability).
use_for: Guidelines and regulation: current international consensus on what explainability and traceability require of clinical AI
verified_how: Crossref record + BMJ landing page (summary and recommendations) + BMJ correction notice
flags: A correction (BMJ 2025;388:r340, 17 Feb 2025) only fixes the spelling of a consortium member's name. The 49 named authors publish with the FUTURE-AI Consortium as a group; the exact wording of the group byline was not checked. Crossref gives no issue number.

title: TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods
key_finding: Reporting guideline with a 27-item checklist (52 subitems) plus a 13-item abstract checklist for prediction-model studies using regression or machine learning; it supersedes TRIPOD 2015, which the authors say should no longer be used. Developed through a modified Delphi (200 respondents from 27 countries in round 2) and a consensus meeting, it adds explicit fairness items across sections, an open-science item (protocol, registration, data and code sharing) and a patient and public involvement item. It does not set a specific explainability requirement, noting only that machine learning models often cannot be reduced to a simple equation and so need fuller reporting.
use_for: Reporting standards for AI prediction models; shows that current reporting guidance stresses fairness and openness more than explanation
verified_how: Crossref record + BMJ landing page (abstract, summary points, methods)
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document, allowed by task). A correction notice dated 18 Apr 2024 (DOI 10.1136/bmj.q902) exists; its content was not read. Delphi participation figures come from the Methods section, not the abstract.

title: Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM): 2024 Update
key_finding: Delphi-based update of the CLAIM checklist by a panel of 73 recruited experts (72 completed both rounds), giving 44 items each answered Yes, No or Not Applicable. It replaces 'ground truth' with 'reference standard', discourages the bare word 'validation' in favour of 'internal testing' and 'external testing', deletes the old data-dictionary item and adds an item on image acquisition protocol. Item 31 asks authors to describe the methods used to explain or interpret model results, give their parameters and state how those methods were validated in the study.
use_for: Reporting standards for imaging AI: the specific CLAIM requirement to report and validate explainability methods
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page (full special report)
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document, allowed by task). Byline is the seven named authors 'for the CLAIM 2024 Update Panel'; Crossref additionally lists the 72 panel members as authors (not included here). No abstract in Crossref; content read on the publisher page.

title: Guiding AI in radiology: ESR's recommendations for effective implementation of the European AI Act
key_finding: ESR AI Working Group statement on how the EU AI Act applies to imaging. Medical-device AI falls in the high-risk class; Article 13 obliges providers to give deployers clear instructions on intended purpose, performance, limitations and oversight measures, for which the ESR recommends model cards; Article 14 requires trained human oversight, with warnings about automation bias and deskilling; and under Article 26 any radiologist or department using AI clinically is a deployer who must follow instructions, supervise, monitor, keep logs and inform patients. The statement notes that methods and standards for transparency and explainability are still under development and asks the European Commission for sector-specific implementation guidance.
use_for: Regulation: EU AI Act transparency and human-oversight duties as read by European radiology
verified_how: Springer landing page (full statement) + Crossref record
flags: Article type is a society statement; the European Society of Radiology is listed as a group author.

authors: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
title: Transparency for Machine Learning-Enabled Medical Devices: Guiding Principles
journal: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (web publication, Center for Devices and Radiological Health)
key_finding: Joint FDA, Health Canada and MHRA principles defining transparency as the degree to which appropriate information about a machine learning-enabled medical device (intended use, development, performance and, when available, logic) is clearly communicated to relevant audiences. 'Logic' is information on how an output was reached and 'explainability' is how well that logic can be understood by a person, so both are treated as aspects of transparency, to be provided 'when available' rather than as a stand-alone mandate. The principles are organised as who, why, what, where, when and how, and rest on human-centred design and on the 2021 good machine learning practice principles 7 and 9.
use_for: Regulation: how North American and UK regulators define transparency and explainability for ML devices
verified_how: FDA web page read in full
flags: Regulatory web document, not a journal article; no DOI, volume or pages. Date recorded is the page's 'content current as of' date (13 June 2024); the page metadata also carried an inconsistent later timestamp. Published 2024 (current standard document). Authorship is institutional.

title: Distinguishing between Rigor and Transparency in FDA Marketing Authorization of AI-enabled Medical Devices
key_finding: Special report separating validation rigour (quality of the evidence the FDA reviews) from validation transparency (how much of it the public can see). Of 1,247 AI marketing authorisations counted, 95.8% (1,195) went through the 510(k) pathway and 76.7% (956) were radiology devices; most radiology AI relies on retrospective standalone or reader studies, and no autonomous radiology AI device has yet been authorised. The authors recommend mandatory, checklist-based reporting of performance validation in 510(k) summaries, a public third-party performance database, reader studies for image-generating AI and prospective studies for future autonomous devices.
use_for: Regulation: limits of public transparency about FDA-cleared radiology AI
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page (full text)
flags: Counts and percentages come from the article body rather than the short abstract. The paper addresses transparency of validation evidence, not model explainability as such.

title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement from the ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR & RSNA
key_finding: Joint statement of five radiology societies (USA, Canada, Europe, Australia and New Zealand) on evaluating, buying, deploying and monitoring radiology AI. It describes many deep learning systems as black boxes, says transparency about purpose, operating conditions, limitations and expected accuracy must be balanced against privacy, proprietary and security risks, and proposes that poor explainability be offset by a higher evidence bar (external or multi-centre data, prospective real-world evaluation). It also calls for local AI governance with periodic re-testing on local data (at least yearly) and drift monitoring, and warns of automation bias.
use_for: Multi-society position on transparency, explainability, monitoring and automation bias in radiology AI
verified_how: Springer landing page (full text, first 100,000 characters) + Crossref record

The same statement was published in parallel in other society journals (search results showed versions in Radiology: Artificial Intelligence, Canadian Association of Radiologists Journal and Journal of Medical Imaging and Radiation Oncology); only the Insights into Imaging version was opened, so cite that one or verify the others separately. title: On the practical, ethical, and legal necessity of clinical Artificial Intelligence explainability: an examination of key arguments
journal: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
key_finding: Systematized review of the arguments for and against requiring explainability in clinical AI. The authors conclude that fully autonomous black-box algorithms are persuasively ruled out on fundamental-rights and justice grounds, but that the published arguments do not establish a general explainability requirement for clinician-in-the-loop use, because lack of explanation does not by itself undermine clinicians' due diligence. They hold that trust should rest on transparency of development and sound clinical decision-making.

title: Fleischner Society: Glossary of Terms for Thoracic Imaging
key_finding: Fourth edition of the Fleischner Society consensus glossary, replacing the 1984, 1996 and 2008 versions. Terms were revised because some are new, some obsolete and others inconsistently used; related terms are grouped under thematic headings, signs and eponyms are reduced in favour of descriptive terms, each term is labelled as anatomy, physiology or pathology, and many more radiograph and CT images are included, with recommended usage given for controversial terms. Its stated aims include standardised communication, structured reporting and database searching.

title: ACR Lung-RADS v2022: Assessment Categories and Management Recommendations
key_finding: Citable article for the 2022 revision of the ACR Lung-RADS system for reporting and managing screen-detected lung nodules, tracing it from version 1.0 (2014) and 1.1 (2019). The v2022 changes add guidance on atypical pulmonary cysts, juxtapleural nodules, airway-centred nodules and findings that may be infectious, clarify how nodule growth is defined, and introduce stepped management for nodules that are stable or decreasing in size, with the supporting evidence and expert consensus summarised.

title: The Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) and Image Database Resource Initiative (IDRI): A Completed Reference Database of Lung Nodules on CT Scans
key_finding: Describes the public LIDC-IDRI database of 1,018 thoracic CT cases assembled by seven academic centres and eight imaging companies. Each scan was annotated by four experienced thoracic radiologists in two phases (blinded read, then unblinded review of all four sets of marks) using three categories: nodule 3 mm or larger, nodule smaller than 3 mm, and non-nodule 3 mm or larger. In total 7,371 lesions were marked as a nodule by at least one radiologist, 2,669 of them in the 3 mm-or-larger nodule category by at least one reader.
use_for: Imaging vocabulary and data: the reference dataset whose radiologist-rated nodule attributes underlie most concept-based chest CT XAI work
